How drought and oil expansion are eroding livelihoods in Iraq's Hawizeh Marshes Submitted by Tamara Imad on Wed, 09/02/2026 - 20:57 As the Unesco-protected wetlands dry up, residents who have long depended on this fragile ecosystem are being pushed out " class="video-embed-field-lazy container-element"> Off In a corner of Halima Flaih’s property in the Iraqi village of Abu Khasaf, just steps from her family’s home, a small concrete structure sits empty under the blazing sun. Flaih and her daughters molded each concrete block by hand. Her husband raised the walls, and she plastered the interior, slowly building out a small gathering space where friends and family could come together, connect, and mark special occasions. Today, the roof is gone, having collapsed due to years of harsh weather and neglect. The land supporting this tiny structure is cracked and dry - a product of a changing climate, exacerbated by a series of state decisions that critics say have prioritised oil extraction over the ecological needs of this sensitive region. Yet Flaih and her family refuse to leave. Instead, they are planning to transform this empty room into a monument to the past - to the life their family once knew here, on the edges of the Hawizeh Marshes. “If the water does not return, future visitors and our children must still learn how the Ma’adan lived in harmony with these wetlands,” Flaih tells Middle East Eye. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); The micro-museum that she plans to create here would showcase traditional marsh culture, including bariya mats hand-woven from wild reeds, fishing nets crafted from cotton threads, and oars for the mashoof, the narrow canoe used by the Ma’adan people to navigate local waters. More than simply preserving the structure her family built by hand nearly two decades ago, Flaih hopes to create a resilient archive of a community pushed to the brink. It will not just be a collection of artifacts, she explains; it will be a last stand against the permanent erasure of the Ma’adan identity. “This room is a living extension of everything my family and I have endured. It is the sole reason we stay,” Flaih says. “We want every visitor to see the profound bond we share with this land … and protect the oral heritage we have carried through centuries, before it is lost forever.” Unique sanctuary Around 350 kilometres southeast of Baghdad, the Hawizeh Marshes stretch across the shared border between Iraq and Iran . A decade ago, these ancient wetlands were inscribed onto the Unesco World Heritage list, recognised as a cradle of human civilisation and a unique sanctuary for biodiversity. The marshes have survived for millennia through the delicate, symbiotic relationship between the ecosystem and local residents - particularly women, whose work has long formed the community’s economic and social backbone. From milking water buffaloes to produce the clotted cream known as qaymar, to weaving bariya mats and hauling in nets of fish to sell in neighbouring urban markets, women have sustained their families here for generations. But today, that way of life is at risk of disappearing. Years of drought have ravaged the fragile landscape in a region where temperatures can approach 50C in the summertime. Intense development activities, including upstream dams and the expansion of oil facilities, have further choked off the water flow to these vital wetlands. Halima Flaih weaves a traditional reed mat in the courtyard of her home on the edges of the Hawizeh Marshes, in Iraq's Maysan governorate, in March 2026 (MEE/Tamara Imad) (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Some residents believe they are being deliberately pushed out to make way for heavy industry. “The earthen berms [the state has] built to protect their wells and facilities blocked the water from us, and their operations consume water allocations,” Flaih’s son, Mustafa, tells MEE, noting that his family must now purchase drinking water to meet their daily needs. “They took the riches of our land and left us to buy a drop of water.” According to research published this March by the London School of Economics Middle East Centre, a massive earthen berm built around the marshes in 2022 - a state initiative officially framed as a measure to combat cross-border drug smuggling - significantly curtailed water inflow, with clear consequences: “Dust replaced water, reeds collapsed, buffalo herds sickened, and entire communities [were] pushed toward displacement.” Hundreds of families from four local villages have been driven out in recent years, researchers noted, calling it a “catastrophe by design”. By 2024, one-fifth of Iraq’s environmentally displaced population hailed from Maysan governorate, where the Hawizeh Marshes are situated. Although Iraqi officials have publicly denied a link between oil development and the depletion of the wetlands, a recent investigation by Daraj Media found that several oil and gas licences overlap with Hawizeh and other protected areas in the country’s south. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); The Chinese company Geo-Jade Petroleum was awarded a contract to develop one of these fields, HWZ 1, located in the Hawizeh Marshes. The oil extraction area overlaps the Unesco-protected zone by 300 square kilometres, according to Save the Tigris, a civil society advocacy group promoting water justice in the Mesopotamian basin. A document from the oil ministry’s legal department, obtained by MEE, shows that while Geo-Jade’s 20-year investment contract entered into force in 2023, environmental assessment work was not completed until the following year, after field operations had already begun, according to local observers. The environmental impact study has not been publicly released. Hauling water Other government documents obtained by MEE shed further light on the encroachment. In March 2025, Iraq’s state-run Oil Exploration Company sent a letter asking the water resources ministry to facilitate exploratory work in the Hawizeh Marshes, including the creation of 10-metre-wide pathways and the drilling of power points. A subsequent letter from the water ministry confirmed that the location of the requested work overlapped the Unesco-protected core zone. MEE reached out to Iraq’s oil ministry and representatives of Geo-Jade for comment on the nature and timing of this work, and asked for clarification on what steps were being taken to mitigate potential harms, but did not receive any response. Hussein Ali al-Kinani, director general of the Centre for the Restoration of the Iraqi Marshes and Wetlands at the water resources ministry, said the state actively monitors infrastructure to protect the ecosystem. Resident Hashem al-Sarray crosses one of the primary waterways that has historically fed Iraq's Hawizeh Marshes, in March 2026 (MEE/Tamara Imad) “Our field teams in Maysan closely track the compliance of the Ministry of Oil and its subsidiary companies to ensure no activities take place within the boundaries of the Hawizeh Marshes, or negatively impact its feeder channels and hydrological regime,” Kinani told MEE. He explained that a joint high-level committee comprising representatives of the water, oil and environment ministries, among others, regularly reviews spatial overlaps between oil concessions and wetland sanctuaries. “If any earthen berms or oil installations are proven to obstruct water flow or divert natural pathways, directives are issued to halt those activities and rectify the damage,” Kinani said, noting that feeder water supplying the marshes “is not used in oil injection operations”. 'Government tankers came maybe once or twice to serve a tiny fraction of the village, but then vanished' - Murtadha al-Janoubi, environmental activist Addressing the severe socioeconomic toll of the drought on indigenous communities, Kinani noted that the government’s emergency response includes dispatching water tankers to ensure villagers can meet their daily needs. But locals on the ground describe a starkly different reality. In Abu Khasaf, residents say government water tankers are virtually non-existent, with families spending up to 60,000 Iraqi dinars ($45) daily for small private water trucks to keep themselves and their remaining buffalo herds alive. “The drought has continued for nine months without a drop of water in the river,” Murtadha al-Janoubi, a local environmental activist, told MEE. “Government tankers came maybe once or twice to serve a tiny fraction of the village, but then vanished.” According to Flaih’s son, Mustafa, “we have to haul water ourselves on motorised tricycles using plastic jerrycans. We never received a single drop from state-funded tankers. The reality is that they leave us to buy our own survival.” 'Devastating impact' Opposition has been growing among local activists, who warn that oil exploration in this area risks damaging an ecological treasure. In April, Save the Tigris sent a letter to Unesco noting that because of the fragility of the marshland ecosystem, such activities “would have a devastating impact”. The exploratory work coincides with “a near-complete cessation of water flow from the Karkheh River in Iran” due to dam-building, the group added, calling on Iraqi authorities to establish an immediate ban on all oil-related activities around the Hawizeh Marshes, and to begin restoration work on areas affected by desiccation and oil projects. In addition to HWZ-1, Save the Tigris pointed to the impacts of oil installations on the adjacent Halfaya field, where pumping stations take in large amounts of freshwater, further drying up the marshlands. Flaih's family lives a few kilometres from the Halfaya oil field (MEE/Tamara Imad) Satellite imagery of the Hawizeh Marshes obtained by AFP from Planet Labs last year revealed visible tracks from heavy vehicles. One resident told the news agency that he saw workers laying cables and drilling holes, while leaked photographs and videos geolocated by the Guardian appeared to show excavators and pipelines in the heart of the protected zone. “The situation on the ground signals a complete catastrophe,” Janoubi said. He has collected photo and video evidence of heavy machinery “operating deep inside the Hawizeh oil field” near the core protected zone, along with footage of oil leakage from another site in Maysan governorate. The Iraqi constitution guarantees all citizens the right to live in a healthy environment, while explicitly safeguarding the country’s biodiversity. But critics say the state is now at risk of violating these commitments - both by allowing oil companies to directly encroach on the marshlands, and by fuelling air pollution, a byproduct of heavy industry. Poverty, displacement and 300 storms: How 'climate violence' threatens Iraq Read More » According to the Netherlands-based NGO Pax, dozens of pollution sources are present in Maysan governorate, generating an annual climate impact equivalent to 22 million metric tonnes of carbon dioxide. IQAir, a Swiss air quality technology company, ranked Iraq as the world’s 11th-most polluted country in 2025. Methane plumes and gas flaring contribute significantly to emissions in Iraq’s south. Ameer Hassoun, a spokesperson for Iraq’s environment ministry, told MEE that the government monitors violations by oil companies and their health impacts, and issues legal warnings for non-compliance. He declined to provide specific data on the number of warnings issued over the past year or whether companies had ultimately complied. Protecting the marshlands and surrounding communities by upholding global environmental standards is a key priority for the ministry, Hassoun added. He did not respond to specific questions about the threat posed by oil exploration within the Hawizeh Marshes. Janoubi said the Iraqi state’s response on this issue has been insufficient, noting that concerted action to restore water flow to the marshlands “is the only way to preserve what is left of our biodiversity”. He added: “If the government is truly serious about saving what remains of the marshes, it must immediately halt all current and future oil expansions, and grant the wetlands their rightful water allocations.” Driven out While Flaih’s family wages a stubborn battle to remain on their land, thousands of others have already been driven from the southern marshlands into an unforgiving expanse of urban sprawl. According to 2024 data from the International Organization for Migration, which began tracking these trends in 2018, more than 140,000 people across central and southern Iraq have been displaced due to climatic and environmental factors. Of the more than 23,000 families affected, around 5,200 hailed from Maysan governorate. Among them are Abu Qasim and Um Qasim, who were forced to pack their belongings in 2022 after the devastation of their buffalo herd. They have since settled in a semi-agricultural area on the outskirts of Amarah city, trading the open horizon of the marsh for a dilapidated house with narrow concrete walls. Rent, which costs them roughly $200 a month, is a heavy burden. Um Qasim and Abu Qasim are pictured at their home in the Hawizeh Marshes in 2022, shortly before the devastation of their buffalo herd forced them to leave (Supplied photo) Once a qaymar artisan, Um Qasim’s daily activities are now limited to caring for their few remaining buffaloes, which live in a small mud pen behind their home. Her sons work in the city market, selling fruits and vegetables for $10-25 on the best days. “It feels like being cast into a foreign country - an alienation I can barely put into words,” Um Qasim tells MEE. “We were never used to this life, these city lights, the roads, or this entire way of living. We spent our lives in a quiet, isolated paradise where even a single car rarely passed by. Moving here disrupted everything we knew.” 'We spent our lives in a quiet, isolated paradise where even a single car rarely passed by. Moving here disrupted everything we knew' - Um Qasim, displaced resident The family must also grapple with social stigma, Abu Qasim says bitterly, noting that some neighbourhoods refuse to sell or rent homes to any family of marsh origin. The Ma’adan are accused of “ruining the city and bringing buffaloes”, he explains, as city residents blame displaced Iraqis for the area’s decayed infrastructure. Their ultimate dream is to pack up and return to the Hawizeh Marshes, as soon as the water is flowing again. But time is running out. Last year, citing third-party reports of oil exploration within the Hawizeh Marshes, Unesco warned that the site’s heritage status could be at risk. The agency’s World Heritage Committee expressed “significant concern over the continued vulnerability of the marsh components and the related natural values of the property to oil and gas developments”, adding that “extractive activities are incompatible with World Heritage status”. It called on the state to “extend its commitment to a permanent ban on all extractive industries within the property”, and to provide an update on the matter by December this year. Heritage status deteriorating According to the International Union for Conservation of Nature’s World Heritage Outlook , which provides regular assessments on the status of protected sites, the outlook for the marshlands of southern Iraq has grown increasingly grim in recent years: from a rating of “significant concern” in 2020, it deteriorated in 2025 to “critical” - the highest threat level. A Unesco spokesperson told MEE that the agency was “very aware of the concerns” about oil and gas development in the Hawizeh Marshes, and that it was “closely monitoring its state of conservation”. A monitoring mission in 2027 will “allow the assessment of progress achieved towards implementing the recommendations to conserve the site, including to re-evaluate whether the property then meets the criteria for its inscription on the List of World Heritage in Danger ”, the spokesperson added. Such a move would enable the World Heritage Committee to mobilise international technical and financial support for its protection. Adel al-Mukhtar, an Iraqi water expert and former adviser to the parliamentary agriculture committee, told MEE that the drying of the marshlands was not merely an inevitable outcome of climate change, but a direct product of what he calls “the absence of effective water diplomacy” with neighbouring states, alongside the government’s failure to mandate a fixed, legally protected water quota for the wetlands. Continuing to prioritise aggressive oil expansion over the sensitive marshlands could mark the end of this once-thriving ecosystem, while threatening to erase the cultural and economic existence of one of the world’s oldest sustainable communities, he added. Mohammed Khidr Mohammed al-Jubouri, an Iraqi consultant specialising in environmental and climate issues, said the risk of irreversible ecological damage hangs heavy. The creation of wide elevated pathways in the core zone of the Hawizeh Marshes - as documented by local activists - could disrupt their natural hydrological flow, he told MEE. “They create stagnant zones, drying out entire sections while flooding others, which decimates spawning grounds for fish and destroys native plant life. It fragments the habitat, physically isolating wildlife populations and severely crippling the reserve’s biodiversity,” Jubouri said. The potential for oil leaks and ruptures near the protected areas is also a concern, as this could contaminate the groundwater and saturate the soil with toxic compounds, destroying the micro-ecosystems responsible for natural water purification, he added. “In waterlogged, anaerobic conditions, these toxins decompose at an agonisingly slow rate,” Jubouri said. “The soil remains a continuous source of poison for years, making natural recovery virtually impossible.” Helpless onlookers Back in Abu Khasaf, Flaih wistfully recalls the historic role of women before the onset of engineered drought across their land. “We made everything from nothing,” she says, describing the production of al-matal, a traditional biofuel made by gathering buffalo and cattle dung, mixing it with straw, and shaping it into circular patties that dry under the sun. This fuel has long been a vital component of heating and cooking during harsh winters, with the patties capable of burning for hours to bake rice-flour bread or to grill fish. Supporting six children alongside her husband, Flaih primarily built her livelihood around the weaving of massive bariya mats, which sometimes reached 10 metres in length, from long wild reeds. She sold them in urban markets for around 10,000 Iraqi dinars ($8) apiece. The ongoing drought did not just choke waterways, she explains; it paralysed women’s hands, turning once-proud producers into helpless onlookers awaiting an unknown fate. With many families now pushed to the impoverished concrete peripheries of Iraq’s southern cities, their ancestral knowledge is of increasingly little use. Flaih and her family are planning to transform this empty structure into a micro-museum to preserve Ma’adan heritage (MEE/Tamara Imad) Flaih and her family are resisting such a life of urban exile, but each day, staying on their land becomes a little bit harder. Her husband, Hashem al-Sarray, recalls the days when the marshlands teemed with fresh water and green reeds, providing ample food for the buffalo herds. The last time he remembers such abundance was more than five years ago, in 2021, before successive waves of drought devastated their land. Back then, Sarray owned more than 20 water buffalo, but he gradually lost half of them to thirst and disease - caused, he believes, by the animals drinking from unsanitary pools of water after the wetlands were depleted. He then sold several others off to afford feed, and trucked-in drinking water for the rest of the herd. 'Selling one buffalo just to buy water to keep the others alive is a slow suicide for our livelihood. There is no profit left here' - Hashem al-Sarray, resident But the quality of their milk plummeted sharply in the absence of natural food sources, collapsing the process of qaymar production that Flaih and her daughters once relied on as another financial lifeline. “We are burning through our savings to buy water and feed for animals that are dying anyway,” Sarray tells MEE. “Selling one buffalo just to buy water to keep the others alive is a slow suicide for our livelihood. There is no profit left here - only a desperate struggle to protect the last ten [animals].” Their eldest son, Mustafa, 23, has now become the family’s main breadwinner. Every day, he travels an hour each way by motorcycle to work at a power plant in Amarah. His daily wage is around $15, barely enough to cover expenses for his siblings’ education and the cost of household water, once obtained freely from the wetlands. Attending classes has become a chore for his two high-school-age siblings. Where they once boarded a mashoof and glided across still waters to their school around two kilometres away, they must now walk a longer route on foot, amid swirling dust and intense heat. Mustafa still prefers this to the alternative. Leaving the marsh, he says, “means dying another way, in urban slums”. This article was produced as part of the 2026 Middle East Eye Fellowship. A Lebanese bank heist towers over this winter's Middle Eastern film offerings Submitted by Joseph Fahim on Fri, 10/30/2026 - 10:42 Rami Kodeih's Furies is set during Lebanon's liquidity crisis of 2019, which led depositors to hold up banks to access their money Rym Mroue (left) and Maria Nakouzi (right) star in Furies, which premiered at Venice (Smokehouse Pictures) Off This has been a middling year for Middle Eastern cinema . With Palestine continuing to dominate the region’s cultural discourse and festivals growing increasingly narrow-minded in their selections, critics and audiences alike have found it difficult to get excited about films that offer little surprise and more of the same habitual subjects. There’s a growing disjunction between local audiences for Middle Eastern films and their international counterparts. Middle Eastern viewers crave seeing their lives represented truthfully, insofar as censorship allows. The incessant stream of familiar fest-bait stories about poverty, war, illegal migration, and toxic patriarchy has little of value to them. International viewers, by contrast, are often drawn to the region precisely because of their familiarity with such representations. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); The decades-long indoctrination of identical narratives and unchanging archetypes into the minds of international viewers has left many with little capacity to accept and enjoy straightforward genres with social commentary delivered in a purer form than that typically catered to by festivals. Preserving artistic integrity while channelling different forms to suit the politics being addressed is the biggest challenge facing visionary artists. What is exceptional about the Middle Eastern films of the autumn and winter seasons is their desire to rework genres into new hybrids that offer ample rewards for both international and local audiences. The overall results may not be entirely successful, but the sheer enterprise of the attempt should be celebrated. Furies For the past seven years, Lebanese cinema has been waiting for a bolt of energy to jolt it out of its doldrums. The debut feature of Beirut-born, Los Angeles-based Rami Kodeih could very well be the film to revitalise a stuttering Lebanese film scene: angry, frantic, uncouth, Furies is a heist thriller realised with a rare mix of panache and perceptiveness. Inspired by the bank robberies carried out in 2019 by ordinary citizens seeking to retrieve their frozen life savings in the wake of the Lebanese economic crisis, the story centres on sisters Maro (Rym Mroue), a hairdresser and single mother, and Dalia (Maria Nakouzi), an employee at a water-truck company and occasional sex worker. 'Mugged and robbed': Worried Lebanese turn to buying guns amid soaraway crime Read More » When Dalia is diagnosed with uterine cancer, Maro attempts to withdraw her money from the bank, but an apathetic manager turns her down, informing her that under such extraordinary circumstances, the bank is not legally bound to serve its clients. With her sister’s life on the line and no justice system she can turn to, Maro decides to take the law into her own hands and rob the bank with the aid of Sunshine (Issam Bou Khaled), an elderly former Phalangist fighter turned neighbourhood helper, and Hamza (Hasan Akil), a co-worker of Dalia’s who is in debt to a local mobster. Few films have managed to convey the pulse, colours, and soul of the Lebanese capital as vividly and lovingly as Furies . Kodeih paints Beirut as a decaying city with a population on perpetual steroids: shouting, quarrelling, embracing, exploiting, and supporting one another. In his astute characterisation and keen eye for capturing the minute details of Beirut life - the food, the blaring pop music, the unmaintained architecture, the distinctive fashion - Kodeih brilliantly conveys the spirit of a city. It is a Beirut defined by glaring contradictions: communal solidarity and sectarian discord; the breakneck speed of daily life and the stagnation of its corrupt politics; the childlike hope for a better tomorrow and the resignation to a state that will never change. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); No other film in the post-2019 mass-uprising era has captured the depth of frustration and fury over what government-backed banks did to the Lebanese people, or the unbearable injustice inflicted by a failed and fractured political system that has never been held accountable. For those who have experienced a similar indignity at the hands of their impotent governments, Furies offers a cathartic experience, fronted by jaded characters who can no longer take it. Kodeih does not shy away from the uglier facets of Lebanese reality - the hyper-realistic skirmish between Christians and Sunnis serves as a reminder that sectarian affiliation continues to shape social interactions 35 years after the end of the civil war. Furies is not perfect. The relationship between the two sisters lacks depth, and the car chase in the final stretch of the picture is awkwardly staged, but these are minor quibbles for an ambitious project that entertains, provokes, and emotionally immerses with a confidence and unassuming quality rarely glimpsed in Lebanese cinema of the 21st century. It is highly commendable and possibly the best Arab film of 2026. A Bit of Light Ali Asghari is swiftly becoming one of Iran’s most internationally acclaimed filmmakers: a bold voice documenting the impact of new and old political maladies on a diverse populace in perpetual change. His latest production - miraculously written, shot, and edited in the immediate aftermath of the burgeoning war - is the opposite in tone and aesthetics to last year’s incisive satire, Divine Comedy : a reimagining of Abbas Kiarostami’s iconic Taste of Cherry , set in Tehran in February 2026, days before the American and Israeli strikes on the country. Unfolding over the course of 24 hours, the film follows Arash (Misagh Zareh), an idealistic physician who decides to kill himself. Still haunted by the treatment of protesters during the 2025-26 demonstrations and the repressive measures the government forced upon him while he was attempting to save them, Arash has been struggling with unbearable guilt and a terminal sense of futility he can no longer live with. A Bit of Light was filmed in the aftermath of US-Israeli strikes on Iran (Seven Springs Pictures) In Arash’s spry city odyssey, Asghari shows a city and a people determined to carry on despite the looming devastation. Torn between the brutality of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps and the barbarism of the American-Israeli siege, Tehran’s middle class finds refuge in art, empathy, solidarity, and resilience with one another. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); The forthcoming attack acts as a recurring comic motif in the story. Arash’s doorman volunteers to put adhesive tape on his office’s windows to protect him from the strikes - an ironic act that several other characters also adopt. The doorman reassures Arash that the US will only target strategic locations and will not harm civilians because “Trump won’t lie!”. Asghari’s perfectly calibrated mix of gallows humour and pathos provides a deeply humanistic and grounded view of a society on the brink of apocalypse. As worn-out individuals like Arash reach their wit’s end, the director poses a central question facing every free-thinking person residing under an authoritarian regime: in the midst of this pervasive violence, how can you carry on? Asghari doesn’t offer any easy answers, but in the brief moments of consoling interactions - a dinner, a reading, a touch, a dance - this bit of light can maybe, just maybe, get you through the night. Falling House Less convincing is Mohsen Gharaie’s domestic thriller Falling House . Farhad Aslani plays Rachid, a veteran low-level prison guard who gets suspended after being accused of taking bribes. His small family, consisting of his wife and two daughters, is being forced to evacuate their current home, which faces demolition because of a municipal redevelopment project. On hope: What Iranians hold on to in uncertain times Read More » Fighting on multiple fronts, the depleted Rachid is shocked when he learns that his daughter Ensi (Laleh Marzban) is plotting to leave Iran and relocate to Turkey to pursue her modelling career. As his paranoia intensifies, Rachid locks up his family and turns his doomed home into a small prison. A cat-and-mouse game between Rachid and his daughter ensues as the family bonds begin, like their home, to unravel. Affecting in its first half, the unsubtle symbolism of the narrative later grows increasingly tiresome and obvious. Rachid is the palpable, well-intentioned but dim-witted. He is the unwavering embodiment of the terribly familiar toxic patriarchy the women of the story must battle in order to win their freedom. The message is on the nose and the drama is largely one-note; the successive revelations do not disclose unseen dimensions of the characters so much as pile on more details that do little to intensify the suspense. Falling House is a recogniseable allegory for toxic patriarchy (Seven Springs Pictures) Solid performances and plight of the female characters make for an intermittently engaging watch. The contrivance of the plot, however, renders Falling House an oversimplified and derivative interpretation of Iranian reality that has been tackled in the same formulaic fashion countless times before. No Paradise If You Are Killed by a Woman The fifth feature of Iraqi -Norwegian director Halkawt Mustafa is the Kurdish answer to American Sniper , with a female protagonist. On paper, it sounds like a recipe for disaster, but the film ultimately works, emerging as a competent action thriller with a delicious feminist twist. Vyan (Avan Jamal) is a young Kurdish-Norwegian woman who travels to Iraq in 2014 with her family to connect with her roots. Before long, the Islamic State group (IS) captures Mosul, kills her parents, and kidnaps her along with her younger sister. Vyan and her sister are sold into slavery. After some time, Vyan murders her captor, escapes, joins a Peshmerga unit, and transforms herself into the most skilled sniper in the unit after killing more than 100 IS fighters. Scarred, injured, and traumatised upon her return to Norway, Vyan learns that her sister is still alive and has been forced to marry an IS commander. She quickly decides to return to Mosul to save her. Anyone expecting new insights into the fraught subject of IS will be disappointed, for No Paradise is a classical action yarn through and through, albeit a compelling and well-executed genre exercise. But by placing Vyan at the heart of the action, Mustafa restores agency to the women victimised by IS, upending the pendulum of power by pitting Vyan against every male aggressor she encounters. No Paradise counters and defies mainstream Middle Eastern cinema’s dominant conception of the alpha-male action hero, offering a fresh and invigorating twist that nonetheless remains largely confined to rigid narrative conventions that leave little room for greater dimension or depth. Elbaraneya The debut feature of Danish- Egyptian director Ashgan El Hamus is a family drama set in the Egyptian countryside that initially appears to be a documentary, thanks to its naturalistic performances, realistic backdrop, and lack of artifice. But Elbaraneya is a work of fiction, featuring a scripted narrative performed by a cast of mostly non-professional actors and shot in the manner of cinema verite. Hamus’s chosen aesthetic grounds the story in a relatable Egyptian reality - a rarity amid censorship this decade - yet it also exposes the limitations of the director’s filmmaking. The film centres on Amal (Reem Amer), a young pregnant woman residing with her family overlooking a jasmine and wheat farm that has been their main source of livelihood. Elbaraneya was filmed with a cast of largely non-professional actors (Ashgan El Hamus) ​ Their traditional life is threatened when an investor offers Amal’s father money to buy his land in exchange for a more comfortable modern house in Cairo. Vehemently resistant at first, the family begins to entertain the possibility of this transition as they gradually reflect on what the land means to them: a deep-rooted part of their identity, an unsustainable old way of life, or a minor facet of their unshakable family connection. Hamus zeroes in on exceptionally observed details, showing an Egyptian life on the brink of extinction: the old-fashioned 1980s furniture, the open-air, if sparse, hangouts, the absence of private spaces. This is a vision of an impoverished yet self-contained world miraculously untouched by President Sisi’s sweeping neoliberal “progress”. With the absence of work opportunities and the impossibility of class mobility, the youngsters of the village find refuge in TikTok and social media. The virtual world becomes the sole vehicle for unloading the youth’s unrealised dreams. Equally shrewd is Hamus’s employment of music. The phony jubilation of Amr Diab’s manufactured pop is relegated to the background, rendered as listless clamour detached from the reality of Amal and her generation. The unruly electronic shaabi beats of Mahraganat, by comparison, provide the primary soundtrack to their lives: a disordered sound for a discordant generation. Only when Amal ventures into Cairo - a cacophony of disharmonious noises and sights and relentless commotion - in the closing stages of the film do we recognise the grave loss marked by this inevitable transition. For Amal’s family, their fortunes will not change, but their lives, and the simple dynamics of their relationship with one another, may never be the same again. There’s undeniable richness in both the themes and characterisation, yet the unjustifiable adherence to a form rendered so rigidly ends up becoming a straitjacket for the film’s unrealised potential. Different parts of the picture offer ample opportunities for magic, for visual splendour that could have pushed the material to soar. Alas, Hamus’s cinematic timidity robs the film of the fundamental poetry needed to augment both the themes and emotional makeup of the story. There’s lots to admire and laud in Elbaraneya , yet the frustration that has entrapped this writer stems from the conviction that the film had a realistic shot at greatness with more imagination and adventurousness. Instead, it settles for a middle ground that leaves a lot to be desired. Film Discover Post Date Override 0 Update Date Mon, 05/04/2020 - 21:29 Update Date Override 0

Following the revision, HSD will retail at Rs400.67 per litre. The prices are applicable for Oct 30 (Friday), according to the Petroleum Division’s notification. The government continues to levy Rs114 per litre in taxes and duties on petrol and Rs100 per litre on diesel. On Tuesday, Jamaat-i-Islami (JI) chief Hafiz Naeemur Rehman met with Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif in Islamabad to discuss his party’s demand to provide relief to the public by abolishing the levy. The two sides agreed to form a joint committee of the JI and the government to consider the expansion of the ongoing fuel relief scheme , being offered to owners of motorcycles, rickshaws and vehicles of up to 800cc since Sept 17 . For his part, Rehman declared that his party would march to Islamabad in protest of the petroleum levy in mid-November if the government did not announce any major relief by then. On Friday, the Pakistan Petroleum Dealers Association had urged consumers not to resort to panic buying, as excessive purchases could create market distortions. The same day, senators raised concerns over fuel supply even after Minister of State for Finance and Revenue Bilal Azhar Kayani said that there were no supply issues. The price of HSD has come down from a peak of Rs520.35 recorded on April 3. Its price had started rising from Rs281 per litre after the US-Iran war broke out on Feb 28. The petrol price had peaked at Rs458.41 on April 3 after beginning its upward trajectory from Rs266 in the first week of March. Meanwhile, the government has reintroduced a raft of austerity measures in response to rising fuel prices amid the ongoing Middle East conflict. Under these measures, markets are required to close by 9pm, and fuel allocations for official vehicles have been cut by 50 per cent for three months. On Sept 13, PM Shehbaz also announced a “ relief scheme ” for users of motorcycles, autos and vehicles of up to 800cc to “alleviate the burden” of rising global oil prices. Previously, on July 17, Petroleum Minister Ali Pervaiz Malik announced that fuel prices would now be fixed on a daily basis due to fluctuations in international market prices following renewed hostilities between Iran and the US. Prior to this, the government had been announcing weekly revisions to fuel prices since early March, alongside measures for the conservation of fuel amid possible oil supply disruptions due to the ongoing conflict in the Middle East. The federal government in April also announced targeted relief measures to provide subsidised fuel. The petroleum minister stated that the cabinet and the prime minister had decided to give the Oil and Gas Regulatory Authority (Ogra) the responsibility of deciding fuel prices on a daily basis based on international market trends. Petrol is mainly used in private transport, small vehicles, rickshaws and two-wheelers, and changes in its price affect the middle and lower-middle classes. Similarly, changes in diesel prices also impact the public at large, as it is mainly used in the heavy transport sector, power plants and large generators. Petrol and HSD are the major revenue earners, with monthly sales of about 700,000 to 800,000 tonnes, compared to just 10,000 tonnes of monthly demand for kerosene.

IRIS access alone is not legal service, LHC rules. LAHORE: The Lahore High Court has held that merely uploading an appellate order to the Federal Board of Revenue’s (FBR) Inland Revenue Information System (IRIS) does not constitute valid service under the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001. An LHC division bench comprising Justice Mirza Viqas Rauf and Justice Anwaar Hussain decided three connected reference applications led by Tahir Mehmood. The applications challenged three orders of the Appellate Tribunal Inland Revenue, which had dismissed the taxpayers’ appeals as time-barred on the ground that uploading the orders to IRIS constituted sufficient service. In one case, the taxpayer argued that Covid-19 and quarantine following a foreign trip had prevented him from accessing the portal. In the other two cases, the taxpayers said they learned of the Commissioner (Appeals)’ orders only after receiving recovery notices in April 2026, months after the orders had been passed. Justice Anwaar Hussain, who authored the judgement, held that Section 218(1)(d) of the ordinance recognises electronic service only when carried out in the prescribed manner. He observed that Rule 74 of the Income Tax Rules limits an electronic addr­e­ss to a fax number or an email address and requi­res confirmation of transmission. IRIS, by contrast, is an internal, web-based workflow system for tax administration, the judge noted, adding that placing an order in a taxpayer’s account does not establish its transmission to an electronic address as required under the rule. The judge distinguished between accessibility and service, observing that an order may be accessible wi­­thout having been served in accordance with the law. He further held that the limitation period could not begin from an event that the law did not recognise as its starting point. Rejecting the department’s argument that Rule 74 could not restrict the parent provision, the jud­ge said the requirement of service in the “prescribed manner” was part of the ordinance itself. The judge also dismissed the contention that taxpayers were required to routinely monitor IRIS. The judge said the dep­artment could not dismiss the pandemic-related exp­lanation, as the corre­ct­n­ess of the tribunal’s conclusion involved a question of law that the high court was competent to examine. Observing that technology was an instrument of statutory administration ra­­ther than an independent source of statutory au­­thority, the judge said mo­­d­ernisation could not disp­ense with legal safeguards. The court referred to rulings of the Peshawar and Islamabad high courts and the Delhi High Court, as well as Articles 4 and 10A of the Constitution. The bench set aside the impugned orders and dire­cted the tribunal to decide the appeals afresh on merit. Published in Dawn, October 30th, 2026

New provinces to carry heavy cost. ISLAMABAD: A private think tank has found more fiscal faults than benefits of the much-discussed creation of new provinces, advising priority to stronger local governments instead of new provinces if public service delivery was actually intended. In its latest market analysis release on Thursday, Policy Research Institute of Market Economy (Prime) highlighted the additional annual recurring cost of Rs47 billion to Rs57bn in case of creation of two more provinces — South Punjab, Bahawalpur and remaining Punjab — and up to Rs730bn if 30 divisional units were to upgrade to provincial status. “Any proposal for creating new provinces should include a formal fiscal costing exercise before constitutional or legislative changes are pursued”, the think tank said, adding that the costing should estimate the recurring expenditure required for the governor, chief minister, provincial assembly, secretariat, high court and other core institutions, together with the likely NFC resource envelope of each proposed unit. This would make it possible to assess whether the expected administrative benefits justify the additional recurring burden,” it said. If the number of provinces increases to six, South Punjab receives an illustrative allocation of Rs1tr under the existing NFC, while Bahawalpur receives Rs537bn. In case of 30 provinces, allocations differ considerably, ranging from Rs7201bn for Lahore and Rs691bn for Karachi to Rs46bn for Loralai and Rs50bn for Zhob. Thus 11 of the 30 proposed units receive less than Rs150bn per annum. Think tank puts annual recurring bill at Rs47-57bn for two provinces and up to Rs730bn for 30 The estimated annual recurring cost of a new provincial government is Rs22.4bn under the low-cost scenario and Rs25.9bn under the high-cost scenario, therefore Rs47-56bn per annum for two and Rs610-730bn for 30 provinces. Using a 10pc fiscal sustainability benchmark based on the low recurring-cost estimate, 16 of the 30 proposed provinces would remain at or below the threshold, while 14 exceed it. The burden is particularly high in the smallest units: the core provincial structure would absorb around 49pc of Loralai’s allocation, 45pc of Zhob’s and 37pc of Rakhshan’s even under the low-cost estimate. Every proposed province with a population below 1.2 million would require more than one-third of its NFC allocation to finance the core provincial government structure. The findings therefore show that the fiscal implications of restructuring depend strongly on the number and size of the provinces created. Limited restructuring involving relatively large units produces a much smaller recurring burden, whereas several smaller division-based provinces would face disproportionately high administrative costs relative to their expected NFC resources. Therefore, at the fiscal level, creation of new provinces will put additional pressure on fiscal resources of smaller provinces, especially those with lower NFC allocations and constrained revenue generation capacity. A greater portion of their available resources would be consumed by ongoing government expenses, resulting in reduced fiscal room for other provincial spending, such as public service provision and developmental expenditure, the analysis showed. Therefore, the think tank emphasised that provincial restructuring should be evaluated not only in political and administrative terms, but also through a clear fiscal framework. Published in Dawn, October 30th, 2026

Sindh govt to launch internship programme for new graduates next month: Sharjeel. KARACHI: Sindh Senior Minister Sha­r­jeel Inam Memon has announ­ced that an internship programme for fresh graduates is being launched from next month through the iwork4Sindh platform. He said that the programme would provide young people with better opportunities to gain practical experience. He said the Sindh government is taking practical measures to provide employment opportunities to young people and enhance their professional capabilities. “The government wants young people to have an appropriate platform to utilise their abilities and access better opportunities,” he added. Mr Memon added that the next phase of physical short courses for skilled individuals is also being launched on the iwork4Sindh platform in collaboration with companies. These courses will focus on developing young people’s skills in accordance with market requirements, he said, adding that in the present era, traditional education alone is not sufficient, as practical skills and professional training are also of great importance to secure employment. ‘Lawfare’ emerges as new threat to journalists in Pakistan. ISLAMABAD: Pakistan remained deeply hostile to journalism and its practitioners in 2025-26 despite a decline in documented violations against media workers, according to a new report issued by an Islamabad-based media watchdog. “About 10 cases a month [against media personnel], their nationwide spread and severity in the period showed that fewer violations did not mean greater safety,” stated Freedom Network’s latest annual Impunity Report 2026, titled “From Violence to Lawfare: Process as Punishment for Journalists”. Produced with technical assistance from International Media Support (IMS), the report was authored by journalist Adnan Rehmat and Freedom Network Executive Director Iqbal Khattak. It finds that “impunity has evolved from a failure to punish violence into a broader system of coercion”. Peca increasingly used to punish dissent, says Freedom Network report The report was released on Thursday ahead of the International Day to End Impunity for Crimes against Journalists, observed worldwide, including in Pakistan, on Nov 2 each year. “Despite the presence on the statute books of two laws to combat impunity for crimes against journalists, such a finding should be a matter of concern for those at the helm of affairs of the two safety commissions established under these laws,” Mr Khattak said. Cases documented between October 2025 and August 2026 included one work-related killing, three attempted assassinations, 18 threats of murder or harm, 11 assaults, 13 legal actions and 32 threats of legal action. Punjab recorded 49 cases, just over half the total, followed by Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Islamabad and Balochistan. Digital and independent journalists were targeted most often. Victims or their families identified government authorities and officials as alleged instigators in nearly two-thirds of the cases. The report identifies the controversial Prevention of Electronic Crimes Act (Peca) and its increasing use against journalists by the National Cyber Crime Investigation Agency (NCCIA) to punish dissent as “central to this legal siege” of online journalism in the country. ‘Recurring pattern’ A detailed analysis of representative Peca-related cases against journalists reveals a recurring pattern in which allegations of defamation, false information, harassment or reputational harm are channelled through cybercrime procedures, including in cases involving reporting on public expenditure, corruption or official conduct. Even without a confirmed FIR or conviction, the process itself becomes “punitive” through summonses, device scrutiny, travel, legal costs, detention, repeated hearings, and reputational harm, the report says. It adds that relief is commonly limited to bail or procedural protection rather than final vindication. The report also provides guidelines for journalists and other media practitioners facing Peca-related cases to help minimise the harmful effects of legal action. It expresses concern over the lack of institutional safeguards for media workers despite the establishment of two high-powered safety commissions, one at the federal level and the other in Sindh. “The federal journalist protection mechanism is effectively dysfunctional, while the Sindh Commission, although more visible, has limited reach and demonstrated protection impact outside Karachi,” it says. How exposed is Bangladesh to a prolonged Saudi crisis?. Bangladesh is unlikely to see an immediate fall in remittances from Saudi Arabia even as Houthi attacks on the kingdom intensified from early October, but a slowdown in new migration could weigh on inflows in the years ahead. Following the attacks, migration to Saudi Arabia, the largest destination for Bangladeshi workers, has already been disrupted. As of Sunday, 144 direct and transit flights had been affected by prolonged flight restrictions at Saudi airports, disrupting the travel plans of around 22,000 passengers. But economists and manpower experts say remittance inflows are unlikely to be hit immediately because newly arrived migrant workers typically take about a year to start sending significant amounts of money home. According to them, the longer-term impact will depend on the duration of the crisis, the performance of the Saudi economy and demand for labour, particularly in construction. A prolonged crisis that damages the Saudi economy could slow job creation and reduce workers’ incomes. But the outcome is not necessarily negative for the kingdom’s economy. If Houthi missile and drone attacks continue without damaging oilfields and refineries, higher global oil prices could boost Saudi revenues, potentially supporting investment and demand for foreign workers, according to Zahid Hussain, a former lead economist at the World Bank’s Dhaka office. “But everything is uncertain so far,” he commented. Remittances are a major source of foreign currency for Bangladesh, accounting for around 7.5 per cent of gross domestic product, according to World Bank data. Their importance has grown amid volatility in global energy markets following the US-Israel war on Iran , which has sent shockwaves through sectors ranging from agriculture to the garment industry. In the July-September quarter of the current fiscal year, Saudi Arabia remained Bangladesh’s largest source of remittances. Inflows from the kingdom rose to $1.65 billion, up from $1.23bn in the same period of FY26, according to Bangladesh Bank data. The kingdom accounted for 19.2pc of Bangladesh’s total remittance inflows in the first quarter of FY27, compared with 16.26pc a year earlier. During the July-September quarter, overall remittances reached around $8.59bn, with Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) countries continuing to account for the bulk of transfers. Diversifying overseas jobs is becoming urgent The latest disruption shows Bangladesh’s heavy reliance on a handful of overseas labour markets, leaving migrant workers and the economy exposed to regional crises. Since FY2014-15, Saudi Arabia has employed around half of the 9.6 million Bangladeshis who went abroad for work. Workers in the kingdom have sent home an average of $5bn a year. The pressure on migration is already evident. Overseas employment fell 36pc year-on-year to 134,000 in the July-August period this year, following a decline to around 969,000 workers in FY26, the lowest level in five years, according to Bureau of Manpower, Employment and Training data. Tasneem Siddiqui, executive director of the Refugee and Migratory Movements Research Unit (RMMRU), a local think tank, said the crisis exposed the structural weaknesses of the country’s migration sector. “Therefore, rather than relying on piecemeal decisions, we must completely overhaul and diversify the manpower market. Otherwise, one crisis after another will emerge, leaving us perpetually vulnerable,” said Tasneem, also a political science professor at Dhaka University. She said the government needs a long-term strategy to develop skills suited to specific overseas markets and expand employment opportunities beyond traditional destinations. “Long-term strategic planning is essential. Particularly, allocating a mere 0.08pc of the budget for a $35bn remittance sector is grossly insufficient to accomplish meaningful interventions,” she said. Meanwhile, economist Zahid said Bangladesh should target countries facing ageing populations and labour shortages, including Japan and countries in eastern Europe, where demand for workers in nursing, caregiving and manufacturing could offer alternatives to Middle Eastern markets. Sayema Haque Bidisha, an economics professor at Dhaka University, also called for greater diversification of migration destinations, stronger diplomatic engagement and better support for expatriates through overseas missions. She said Bangladesh needs to improve its international image by demonstrating that its workers can fill skilled jobs, rather than being seen primarily as a source of manual labour. Shariful Hasan, associate director of BRAC’s Migration Programme and Youth Platform, said earlier this month that many Bangladeshi workers in Saudi Arabia depend on daily or weekly employment and that security concerns have reduced work opportunities. Pakistan faces greater exposure than India Bangladesh is not the only country with a significant reliance on remittances from Saudi Arabia. Its neighbours India and Pakistan also depend on money sent home by their citizens working in the kingdom, although the potential impact varies. Saudi Arabia is Pakistan’s largest source of remittances, contributing $9.78 billion in the last fiscal year, according to State Bank of Pakistan data. Meanwhile, around 7pc of India’s international remittance inflows originate from Saudi Arabia. The country receives about $8 billion annually from the kingdom, according to the Reserve Bank of India. A prolonged crisis that affects employment and earnings in Saudi Arabia could therefore have a greater impact on Pakistan than on India, given Pakistan’s substantial reliance on the kingdom as a source of remittances.

'You are disgusting': Trump lashes out at reporter as he cancels weekend rallies ahead of midterm polls. US President Donald Trump is scrapping two of his last midterm election rallies, his Republican Party said Thursday, as the 80-year-old leader lashed out at a reporter who asked if he was “sick of travelling”. “You’re sick to ask that question. You are sick,” Trump told the reporter after returning to Washington from a campaign trip to South Carolina. “I feel perfect. You are disgusting. Put yourself in shape, you look like hell.” Trump told reporters he did not “feel like I have to go to Kansas,” a Midwestern state where Senator Roger Marshall, a fellow Republican, is in an unexpectedly competitive race with Democratic challenger Adam Hamilton. “He is doing very well,” Trump said of Marshall. “We are going to have a strong Tuesday night.” Later on Thursday, the Republican National Committee said in a statement that it would also cancel a planned rally in Iowa, home to several competitive congressional races. Instead of the events in Kansas and Iowa, Trump will hold a “large number” of virtual “telerallies” in a series of states, the Republican National Committee said. The canceled in-person rallies were set for Salina, Kansas, on Saturday, and Dubuque, Iowa, on Sunday. Republicans are fighting to keep control of Congress in the November 3 midterms. Trump has urged the party to “pretend I’m on the ballot” to maximise turnout despite his poor approval ratings. “With Republicans in a strong position in Kansas and Iowa, previously planned in-person rallies in those states will no longer take place as scheduled,” the RNC statement said. The president is still expected to travel to rallies in several states before Tuesday’s election. Trump’s final election rally is now set to be in Florida on Friday. Despite being the oldest elected president in US history, Trump has kept up a gruelling schedule of near-daily rallies throughout October to help Republicans in the midterms. Since October 1, Trump has hosted 25 rallies in 19 states, often speaking for his party in rural areas of Republican-friendly states. Tuesday’s midterm elections will determine whether Republicans retain narrow control of the US Senate and House of Representatives. MAGA Inc, a campaign funding group aligned with Trump, said on Thursday it would host a series of “tele-rallies” with the president in at least 19 states, including Kansas and Iowa, before Election Day. Trump has noted that his recent series of more than hour-long campaign speeches has been challenging. Sounding hoarse in Mississippi on Monday, Trump said, “God didn’t make your vocal cords to do a rally every day.” On Thursday, after campaigning for Senator Darline Graham in South Carolina, Trump ridiculed a Reuters reporter who asked how he felt after weeks of rallies and whether he was sick of travelling. “You’ve been following me for two weeks,” Trump said before boarding his motorcade back to the White House. “I feel perfect.”

Cop martyred in KP's Bajaur as terrorists attack police post: official. BAJAUR: A police officer was martyred after terrorists attacked a police post in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa’s Bajaur district, officials said on Friday. The attack on the police post in Silai Pati area in the remote Barang tehsil, bordering Malakand district, occurred late on Thursday night. Mansoor Khan, a spokesperson for the district police, while confirming the attack, told Dawn that a group of Fitna al-Khawarij terrorists targeted the Silai Pati police post, prompting the personnel to retaliate bravely and courageously. LHC directs Noreen Niazi’s counsel to file separate plea for medical treatment, family meetings. LAHORE: The Lahore High Court on Friday directed the counsel for Noreen Niazi, sister of former prime minister and PTI founder Imran Khan, to file a separate miscellaneous application seeking medical treatment and family meetings. On Wednesday evening, Noreen was shifted to the Punjab Institute of Cardiology (PIC) following her deteriorating health conditions, on the recommendation of the doctors of the Kot Lakhpat Jail, where she has been detained. Justice Abher Gul Khan issued the direction while hearing a petition filed by Sakeena Niazi challenging the extension of the preventive detention of PTI founder Imran Khan’s two sisters, Noreen and Dr Uzma Khan. The judge asked the petitioner’s counsel whether an application had been filed seeking permission for medical treatment and meetings with family members. Advocate Rana Mudassar Umar, counsel for the petitioner, replied that an application to this effect had been submitted to the deputy commissioner. The judge directed the counsel to also file a separate civil miscellaneous application with the court. The counsel argued that there was no lawful justification for extending the detention of the two women. He said Noreen, 70, had never suffered from a heart ailment before. Questioning the circumstances that led to her hospitalisation, Advocate Umar asked what kind of pressure had been exerted on her during detention that she had to be taken to hospital. He argued that the fresh detention orders were replicas of the previous ones, with only the dates changed. He further argued that suspending the detention notification would pave the way for the women’s release. PTI Secretary General Advocate Salman Akram Raja, who was also present in court, claimed that Noreen was ill and had been shifted to the hospital’s intensive care unit. However, neither her family members nor her lawyer had been allowed to meet her, he added. He said he was unaware whether she was still in hospital or had been shifted back to jail. Asked whether the home secretary, who was abroad, had returned to the country, Additional Advocate General Nasir Chohan said he would check and inform the court. Another petition, filed by Shahrez Khan challenging the detention of his mother, Aleema Khan, is yet to be fixed for a hearing. Imran’s sisters were detained by authorities in September, under Section 3 of the MPO, as the PTI geared up for a planned protest march towards Islamabad. Their detention was ordered for 30 days and would have expired on Oct 19 for Aleema and Oct 20 for Uzma and Noreen. However, they remained in jail, and the government later informed the LHC that their detentions had been extended on Oct 7. On Sept 24, the LHC had turned down a request to immediately suspend the preventive detention notifications issued against Noreen and Dr Uzma. Earlier this month, Imran’s cousin, Qasim Zaman, was also taken into custody when he went to Adiala jail to meet the ex-prime minister. The detention had come amid reports of a crackdown on the PTI ahead of its countrywide protest and march to Islamabad, which the party had called to demand Imran’s release from jail and mobilise people for the supremacy of the Constitution.

Court grants NCCIA four-day physical remand of suspect in counterfeit US postage stamp scam. LAHORE: A judicial magistrate on Friday granted the National Cyber Crime Investigation Agency (NCCIA) a further four-day physical remand of the prime suspect in a Rs35 billion fraud involving the online sale of counterfeit US postage stamps . The NCCIA produced suspect Faheem Akram and his co-suspect, Naeem, before the court after their previous four-day remand expired. The investigating officer (IO) sought further custody of the suspects for interrogation. Magistrate Naeem Wattoo granted the agency’s request and extended the physical remand of both suspects by four days. The IO was directed to produce the suspects again on Nov 3. The initial investigation revealed that the suspect had allegedly been operating a website since August 2023 through which he sold more than five million counterfeit US postage labels online. According to the US Department of Justice, Akram was indicted by a federal grand jury in Florida in September 2026 over the alleged sale of more than 5.1 million counterfeit postage labels, which prosecutors say caused losses of more than $126 million to the US Postal Service. US prosecutors allege that the website sold the labels for around $2 each, regardless of the weight, size or destination of a package. A US court order authorised the seizure and shutdown of the website. The NCCIA had arrested the suspect, a resident of Khanewal, in Lahore. Money trail In a press conference on Oct 20, NCCIA’s Lahore Zone Additional Director Atif Ameer said that 16 bank accounts had been used in the scam. Seven of the accounts were operated by the suspect, five by his brother, two by his wife, and one each by his sister and aunt. He said the agency had expanded the investigation across several parts of the country. “Eight special teams were formed in Punjab, Islamabad and Sindh to trace the suspect and investigate the network,” he said and added the teams conducted raids at 35 locations and questioned 47 people as part of the investigation. “Investigators also employed digital and forensic techniques to establish the suspect’s movements and identify people associated with the operation.” Ameer added that investigators analysed 122 call-data records, 50 IMEI-tracking reports and audio and video recordings from 120 cameras. “Artificial intelligence and other modern technological tools were also used during the investigation. A locator operation continued for 10 days as investigators attempted to establish the suspect’s whereabouts and trace his activities,” he said. The NCCIA said the major focus of the investigation was the financial trail generated by the online sale of the counterfeit stamps. “We are examining transactions conducted through the 16 bank accounts and attempting to determine the flow of funds between the accounts allegedly belonging to the suspect and his relatives. “The involvement of family members is also being examined as part of the investigation, particularly the alleged use of their bank accounts in connection with the online business,” the additional director said. He said the role of other individuals in operating the website, processing orders, receiving payments or distributing the counterfeit stamps was also being probed. “Investigators are also working to establish the full scale of the operation and verify the volume and value of the transactions,” he said.

PPP delegation calls on Senate opposition leader, urges participation in proposed committee on electoral reforms.
