By 2023, militant attacks had become so regular in Jammu that the government was forced to revive a defunct militia known as the Village Defence Guards, arming and training hundreds of villagers across the region. 71 These militias were first formed in the mid-1990s, at the height of the Kashmiri insurgency, but the government disbanded them when militancy declined. “India revives civil militia after Hindu killings in Kashmir”, AP, 28 February 2023. On 9 June 2024, just hours after Prime Minister Modi was sworn in for a third consecutive term, militants assailed a bus carrying Hindu pilgrims, killing nine and injuring more than 30 in Jammu’s Reasi district. 72 “Terrorist attack at Reasi sets alarm bells ringing in India’s security establishment”, The Diplomat , 20 June 2024. The attack appeared to have been timed to contradict the government’s narrative of a peaceful region open for visitors. 73 Crisis Group noted in 2022 that tourists “could well become targets, particularly if the government continues to insist that robust tourism is a sign of normalcy”. See Praveen Donthi, “ Violence in Kashmir: Why a Spike in Killings Signals Ominous New Trend ”, Crisis Group Commentary, 28 June 2022. Before becoming chief minister, Omar Abdullah also cautioned that by “[linking] tourism with normalcy, [officials] put tourists in danger”. See “Tourist arrivals in Kashmir not an accurate gauge of normalcy: Omar Abdullah”, Business Standard , 20 May 2024. Indian officials, for their part, have blamed the spike in violence in Jammu on Pakistan-based militants sneaking across the border. 74 “Jammu and Kashmir: Surge in attacks brings fear to calmer parts of Himalayan territory”, BBC, 23 July 2024. D. “Foreign Militants” Indian officials say the outfits attacking non-locals in Indian-administered Kashmir (and increasingly in Jammu) are not new, but the same groups that Pakistan has long supported, above all Lashkar-e-Tayyaba and Jaish-e-Mohammad, just with new names. According to New Delhi, both groups rebranded themselves to enable Islamabad to evade scrutiny by the Financial Action Task Force over allegations of funding terrorist groups. 75 The Task Force had until October 2022 placed Pakistan on its grey list for failing to curb money laundering and financing of these outfits. “Pakistan is out of FATF ‘grey list’ on terror funding”, The Hindu , 22 October 2022. Furthermore, Indian officials allege, “foreign militants” have assumed increasing responsibilities in these organisations of late. They claim that the militants allegedly infiltrating Jammu are more dangerous than their predecessors, mainly because they seem well trained and the police cannot track them through family connections. “Some of the old tactics are back”, a retired police chief of Jammu and Kashmir observed, referring to the period from the 1990s to the early 2000s, when Jammu was rife with militancy, and Pakistanis made up a sizeable portion of militant ranks “So we also need to revisit the old tactics and learnings on our side”. 76 “Pak control, narrative war, white-collar terror: Ex-DGP of J&K R. S. Swain’s first big interview”, op. cit. Indian officials also claim that these “foreign militants” have sophisticated weapons, and are adept at avoiding detection, particularly by using encrypted Chinese satellite phones (part of the BeiDou network) whose transmissions are difficult to intercept. 77 Militants have been found using weapons such as U.S.-made M4 assault rifles. Crisis Group interviews, security officials, Jammu and Srinagar, 2025. See also “US arms left in Afghanistan are turning up in a different conflict”, NBC News, 30 January 2023; and “Hard-to-crack Chinese devices part of terror toolkit,” The Economic Times , 30 April 2025. If true, it would be a striking evolution from the years before 2019, when militants were largely untrained and poorly equipped locals. By the end of 2023, Indian forces say, “foreign militants” had come to outnumber local insurgents. 78 “Security situation improved significantly in J&K in 2023; foreign terrorists our target for 2024, says DGP”, The Hindu , 31 December 2023. After the deadly terror attack in Pahalgam in 2025, New Delhi was quick to hold Pakistan responsible, though it has yet to present any concrete evidence to back its accusations. 79 “A year on, India has failed to substantiate allegations against Pakistan over Pahalgam attack: info minister”, Dawn , 22 May 2026. The government’s determination to pacify Kashmir led to broad anti-terror laws, which locals view as collective punishment, fuelling resentment against the Indian state and proving counterproductive. Srinagar, Kashmir, India. November 2025. CRISIS GROUP / Praveen Donthi IV. The India-Pakistan Fault Line Kashmir’s conflict is inseparable from the dispute between India and Pakistan, which have already waged two wars (1947-1948 and 1965) over the territory and made several smaller forays into armed conflict. A third war erupted in 1971, after India intervened militarily on behalf of the Bengali struggle for independence in Pakistan’s eastern wing, which led soon thereafter to sovereignty for Bangladesh. 80 From May to July 1999, the sides clashed in Jammu and Kashmir’s Kargil district, with hundreds of soldiers killed. In 2019, they engaged in short-lived air combat following an attack in Jammu and Kashmir that killed 40 Indian troops. In April 2025, the militant attack on Indian tourists in Pahalgam in southern Kashmir triggered the most serious fighting between the two neighbours in decades, after India blamed Pakistan for the massacre. Four days of hostilities ended with a ceasefire on 10 May. Though New Delhi promised systematic retaliation against Islamabad if further attacks occurred on its soil, it stayed its hand when young Kashmiris carried out a suicide bombing in New Delhi on 10 November 2025. With India continuing to claim that Pakistan uses anti-India jihadist groups to wage a proxy war in Kashmir, another terror attack in the region or elsewhere in India could threaten a fragile ceasefire. A. The Pahalgam Attack and Its Aftermath The 22 April 2025 attack in Pahalgam, which saw militants shoot 26 people at point-blank range at a popular tourist destination in southern Kashmir, was the deadliest attack on civilians in over two decades. Most of the victims were Hindu tourists, whose religion the militants ascertained before gunning them down. 81 The victims also included a local Kashmiri who tried to intervene and an Indian Christian. Praveen Donthi, “Deadly Kashmir Militant Attack Raises Temperature Between India and Pakistan”, Crisis Group Commentary, 25 April 2025. The Indian government immediately blamed Pakistan, alleging that it wanted to “undermine normalcy returning to Jammu and Kashmir”, disrupt the economy and “create a fertile ground for continued cross-border terrorism”. 82 “Transcript of Special Briefing on OPERATION SINDOOR”, Indian Ministry of External Affairs, 7 May 2025. Hours after the attack, New Delhi further downgraded diplomatic ties with Islamabad, shut Indian airspace to Pakistan-registered aircraft, closed the only border crossing and suspended the 1960 Indus Waters Treaty. Islamabad responded in kind. Denying Indian allegations that the Pahalgam assailants had any cross-border connections, Islamabad accused New Delhi of making these charges without evidence, while rejecting Pakistan’s suggestions of an independent international investigation into the attack. 83 On 26 April, Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif said Islamabad was open to participating in any neutral, transparent and credible investigation of the attack. “PM Shehbaz says Pakistan open to credible, transparent probe into Pahalgam attack”, Dawn , 26 April 2025. New Delhi regarded Islamabad’s offer as disingenuous, pointing to its record of supporting anti-Indian jihadist proxies. Islamabad insisted in turn that the Modi government’s belligerent rhetoric was intended to whip up nationalist sentiment as it planned a military attack on Pakistan. 84 Crisis Group Briefing, India-Pakistan: Avoiding a War in Waiting , op. cit. In the immediate aftermath of the attack, Indian forces detained thousands of Kashmiris, informing the media that the attackers had been locals. 85 “If the photographs didn’t belong to the Pahalgam attackers, what were the actions based on?”, Kashmir Times , 4 July 2025. State forces destroyed the houses of at least six suspected local militants. But the National Investigation Agency eventually listed seven accused, including the Pakistan-based heads of Lashkar-e-Tayyaba and The Resistance Front; it concluded that three Pakistanis had carried out the attack, while two local Kashmiris had provided them with food and shelter. 86 “NIA charges four LeT-TRF terrorists in Pahalgam attack”, The Hindu , 16 December 2025. In July 2025, India claimed to have killed all three of the Pakistanis, though without making the evidence public, and arrested the two Kashmiris allegedly involved. 87 Addressing parliament, Home Minister Amit Shah said security forces had established that the assailants were Pakistanis because they found Pakistani voter cards and chocolates made in Pakistan on the bodies. No further evidence was provided. “Three Pakistani terrorists behind Pahalgam terror attack killed in Operation Mahadev, centre tells Lok Sabha”, The Hindu , 29 July 2025. The terror attack on tourists visiting from throughout India, most of whom were shot dead in front of their families, shocked Kashmiris, who organised spontaneous protests condemning the killings. Many locals were also apprehensive about the backlash they knew was coming. Notwithstanding widespread public condemnation of the massacre, a section of Kashmiri society, according to a leading journalist in the region, viewed it as a consequence of New Delhi’s stranglehold on the region. 88 Crisis Group interview, senior Kashmiri journalist, 2025. Throughout the rest of India, the killings provoked a furore, as well as mounting pressure on the government to retaliate against Pakistan. On 7 May, India launched Operation Sindoor, carrying out cross-border strikes on what it claimed was “terrorist infrastructure” across the border. This first salvo gave rise to a short but fierce exchange of fire, in which the two sides carried out tit-for-tat attacks using weaponised drones and missiles deep inside each other’s territory and across the Line of Control, the informal frontier that separates the Indian- and Pakistani-administered parts of Jammu and Kashmir. 89 Crisis Group Briefing, India-Pakistan: Avoiding a War in Waiting , op. cit. The ceasefire froze the conflict, with both sides claiming victory, but it did not stop either from continuing its hostile posturing. After four days of conflict, U.S. President Donald Trump announced that the two countries had agreed to a ceasefire, which Indian and Pakistani authorities confirmed. New Delhi said it was the Pakistani military that had requested the truce through a hotline between the directors general of military operations – the only official line of communication between the two countries. Pakistan claimed that India had reached out to it first. The ceasefire froze the conflict, with both sides claiming victory, but it did not stop either from continuing its hostile posturing. 90 Ibid. Prime Minister Modi declared that India would from now on systematically strike back against not just those perpetrating terrorist attacks on Indian soil, but also their backers – a clear allusion to Pakistan. 91 Ibid. These clashes were traumatic for many Indians, particularly in regions which endured missile and drone strikes for the first time. Many Kashmiris experienced it differently, however. Seeing Pakistani drones in their skies, hovering above and firing upon Indian installations in the region, seems to have made an impression on local people. The display of Pakistan’s military capabilities on the first day of the conflict, when it allegedly shot down several Indian fighter jets, likewise had a notable effect on local public opinion. 92 See “Pak’s Fatah 1 rocket debris fished out of Srinagar’s Dal Lake during clean-up”, India Today , 22 September 2025. “The May conflict countered post-2019 hopelessness that Pakistan is not interested in Kashmir”, a Srinagar resident observed. 93 Crisis Group interview, Srinagar, 2025. B. Weighing the Pakistani Role India insists that Pakistan is responsible for almost all militant attacks in the region, accusing Islamabad of fighting a proxy war in Kashmir, using anti-India jihadist groups such as the Lashkar-e-Tayyaba and Jaish-e-Mohammad. Indian officials also claim that Pakistani fighters are steadily infiltrating Jammu and Kashmir. 94 An Indian security official claimed that there were about 100 foreign (meaning Pakistani) militants in Kashmir. Crisis Group interview, Srinagar, 2025. Concurring with these allegations, a section of Kashmiris also say Pakistan-based jihadist groups, working at Islamabad’s behest, are now spearheading the insurgency in Kashmir. 95 Crisis Group interviews, Srinagar, 2025. Until recently, Kashmiris had disputed Indian government claims, regarding them as simplistic, albeit without denying Pakistani influence. Instead, they pointed to local young people joining militant ranks out of anger at Indian policies toward the region (see Section III.C). Nowadays, however, many claim that Pakistan is back in the driver’s seat. Establishing the truth regarding these allegations is no easy matter. Pakistan categorically denies India’s claims that it is waging a proxy war in Indian-administered Kashmir. 96 “Pakistan takes ‘strong exception’ to ‘baseless claims’ of Indian army chief”, The News , 15 January 2025. It has repeatedly said it opposes any form of terrorism, and it argues it has clamped down on homegrown jihadist groups blamed for terrorist attacks in India. 97 “Nuclear war ‘wasn’t an option’”, Dawn , 14 May 2025; “FO says Pakistan has ‘dismantled’ terrorist outfits amid U.S. designation of group blamed for Pahalgam attack”, Dawn , 18 July 2025. Lashkar-e-Tayyaba was officially banned in 2002, following an attack on the Indian parliament, as was Jaish-e-Mohammad in 2008 after another in Mumbai. When the groups attempted a comeback under new names, these were also outlawed; Lashkar-e-Tayyaba’s charity front, Jamaat-ud-Dawa, was proscribed in 2008 and Jaish-e-Mohammad’s so-called philanthropic arm, the Falah-i-Insaniyat Foundation, in 2019. The next year, the government froze the properties and assets of both groups. Islamabad also says the leaders and activists of these groups are under house arrest or jailed, including Lashkar-e-Tayyaba chief Hafiz Saeed, whom India now holds responsible for the Pahalgam attack. Convicted of terrorism financing in 2019, Saeed is in prison serving a 33-year sentence. 98 Crisis Group Briefing, India-Pakistan: Avoiding a War in Waiting , op. cit. The fact that banned anti-India jihadist groups have proven capable of repeatedly re-emerging, only to be outlawed again, tends to undermine Pakistan’s claims that it has eliminated their organisational structures altogether. That said, it does not constitute definitive proof of New Delhi’s allegations that Islamabad is once again waging a proxy war in Jammu and Kashmir, including by sending in jihadist proxies. Pakistani experts say such a policy would undermine the country’s national security and damage its international standing. 99 Crisis Group telephone interviews, Pakistani analysts, August 2026. Islamabad claims that India is backing proxies fighting Pakistan in [Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and Balochistan provinces]. Top Pakistani policymakers reportedly feel that any armed venture could spark conflict with India, leaving the country open to a two-front threat at a time when it confronts a raging insurgency in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and Balochistan provinces, bordering Taliban-controlled Afghanistan, where militant attacks have killed thousands of Pakistan’s security personnel and civilians. 100 Crisis Group telephone interview, August 2026. See also Crisis Group Asia Report N°354, Pakistan: Responding to the Militant Surge on the Afghan Border , 27 February 2026. Islamabad claims that India is backing proxies fighting Pakistan in these regions via its close ties with the Afghan Talban authorities and support for anti-Pakistani insurgents on Afghan soil, namely Baloch militant groups and the jihadist Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (or Pakistani Taliban). 101 Islamabad, however, holds Kabul primarily responsible, alleging that the Afghan Taliban provide safe havens to Pakistani militant groups. “Naqvi holds India responsible for spate of attacks in Balochistan: ISPR says 92 terrorists killed”, Dawn , 31 January 2026; “DGISPR tells Afghan Taliban regime to choose between terrorist organisations and Pakistan”, Dawn , 27 February 2026. Islamabad’s public response has been to highlight Indian human rights violations in Kashmir in international forums, including at the UN Security Council, calling New Delhi out for what it calls “state-sponsored” terrorism against Kashmiri Muslims. 102 “UNSC condemns Swat suicide blast after Pakistan sounds alarm on Afghan terrorist havens”, Dawn , 6 June 2026. In an implied reference to Indian-administered Kashmir, it has also demanded a clear “distinction between terrorism and the legitimate struggle against foreign occupation and the right of self-determination”. 103 “Pakistan calls for internal reform of UN’s counterterrorism architecture”, Dawn , 2 July 2026. Islamabad has gone on to accuse New Delhi of “weaponising” water, warning that it would have no choice but to act, including militarily, should India store or divert waters allocated to Pakistan under the Indus Waters Treaty. 104 The three western rivers allocated to Pakistan under the treaty supply 80 per cent of the country’s total water consumption. Crisis Group Briefing, India-Pakistan, Avoiding a War in Waiting , op. cit. Despite the rhetoric, the Kashmir dispute appears to have lost much of its prominence in Pakistan as Islamabad’s attention shifts from its South Asian neighbourhood to the Middle East. In September 2025, Pakistan signed a mutual defence agreement with Saudi Arabia, cementing a longstanding partnership; it went on to sign a joint defence agreement with Saudi Arabia and Türkiye the following August. Islamabad has also assumed the mantle of mediator since the outbreak of the U.S.-Iran war, leveraging its strategic and diplomatic links with the U.S., as well as its working relationship with neighbouring Iran. 105 Crisis Group Commentary, “Pakistan: A New Player in the Quest for a U.S.-Iran Breakthrough”, 4 June 2026. As a result, Pakistan would appear to have few incentives and little need to meddle in India, let alone support Islamist jihadist proxies in Kashmir, according to one Pakistani analyst. Pakistani policymakers are said to be well aware that backing a proxy war would corroborate the BJP government’s portrayal of Pakistan as a threat to regional stability and global peace. 106 Crisis Group telephone interview, August 2026. Another prominent Pakistani analyst, however, warned that even the “creeping presence” of anti-India jihadist groups, particularly Lashkar-e-Tayyaba and Jaish-e-Mohammad, should be a matter of concern for Islamabad. So long as the authorities do not rigorously enforce the ban on such groups, India’s claims will not ring hollow. 107 Mohammad Amir Rana, “A New Pakistan”, Dawn , 13 July 2025. C. The Delhi Blast and the Threat of Religious Violence On 10 November 2025, a car laden with explosives blew up at a busy intersection in New Delhi, killing fifteen and injuring more than 30 people. 108 “Delhi car blast: Doctors with bombs”, The Hindu , 18 November 2025. The driver, who died in the blast, turned out to be a Kashmiri doctor, seemingly adding a new dimension to conflict in the region. Investigative agencies claim to have uncovered a “white-collar terror” network, including five other physicians from Kashmir; in all, thirteen individuals have been accused of belonging to it so far, including a woman doctor from the northern Indian state of Uttar Pradesh. All Muslim, they were allegedly attempting to revive Ansar Ghazwat-ul-Hind, an offshoot of al-Qaeda in the Indian Subcontinent. 109 Al-Qaeda’s influence on Kashmiri militancy has been minimal, as Kashmiris consider the group’s ideology too extreme. The presence of a local separatist leadership also reduced the pull of transnational jihadism. Given the Kashmir links, Indian security agencies carried out an extensive crackdown in the Himalayan region, demolishing the suspects’ houses in the process. Despite Prime Minister Modi’s earlier threat to retaliate against Pakistan for every terrorist attack perpetrated in India, the government refrained from immediately blaming Islamabad, possibly out of desire to avoid another war. In the end, the National Investigative Agency concluded the attack was carried out by a group led by medical professionals and inspired by the al-Qaeda splinter rather than Pakistan-backed militants. 110 According to the NIA, the accused formed Ansar Ghazwat-ul-Hind Interim in June 2022, after a failed attempt to travel to Afghanistan, stockpiling arms and ammunition as well as manufacturing explosives using commercially available chemicals. “NIA names three more accused in supplementary chargesheet in Red Fort area blast case”, The Hindu , 27 June 2026. The involvement of physicians in a suicide bombing came as a shock to Kashmiri society. Though militants have carried out suicide attacks in Kashmir in the past and educated individuals have become insurgents, these two trends have rarely overlapped. For now, the attack remains a one-off event, with no evidence that it forms part of a larger trend. That said, it has raised alarm in Kashmir at the prospect that more suicide bomb cells made up of young people may emerge. Though the New Delhi bombers had not previously been jailed, some Kashmiris are concerned that young adults incarcerated under anti-terror laws are being exposed to the influence of hard-core militants and separatist ideologues, and often turn to religion to cope with jail life. 111 Crisis Group interview, Waheed Ur Rehman Para, member of Legislative Assembly, Srinagar, November 2025. Meanwhile, the permanent fear of state surveillance appears to have played a central role in the breakdown of social cohesion and communication in the traditionally close-knit Kashmiri community. 112 “Radicalisation in Kashmir: The ideological transformation”, The New Indian Express , 16 November 2025. “I no longer know how my son thinks or whether he knows about his son”, a former Kashmiri bureaucrat noted, lamenting the fraying of bonds in society. 113 Crisis Group interview, Srinagar, 2025. Investigative agencies claimed that a group of medical professionals from Kashmir was responsible for a suicide blast in New Delhi last November, killing fifteen and injuring many more. Koil, Kashmir, India. November 2025. CRISIS GROUP / Praveen Donthi Two of the doctors were from Koil village in South Kashmir whose homes were demolished by the security forces. Koli, Kashmir, India. November 2025. CRISIS GROUP / Praveen Donthi V. A Way Forward It is becoming increasingly clear that India’s efforts to revamp Kashmir by stamping out resistance and establishing central control of its administration have failed. New Delhi should turn the page by recognising the political dispute at the heart of the region’s unrest, eschewing the temptation to view all militancy through a religious lens and reorienting its approach through a series of steps that would allow it to manage the conflict more effectively. A. Restoring Political Rights Though several indicators of unrest in Jammu and Kashmir have steadily declined, including militant violence, street demonstrations and stone throwing, the region is at constant risk of renewed turbulence. Trying to build stability on a foundation of central rule, heavy-handed law enforcement and counter-insurgency is not the right approach. Despite the BJP government’s claims to the contrary, Kashmiri Muslims believe that the changes imposed since 2019 have been motivated by prejudice in the shape of a Hindu nationalist desire to disenfranchise them. As the 2024 elections show, diverse and hitherto antagonistic political forces in Kashmir, from mainstream politicians to separatists, have come together in response to the perceived threat to the region’s community and way of life. Tacit support for militant groups has also grown among a number of Kashmiris, who have come to think that armed struggle is the only way to prevent India from overhauling the region’s socio-religious identity and robbing it of political autonomy. A continued campaign of militant violence, however, is likely to aggravate tensions with New Delhi and fuel bilateral discord between India and Pakistan, stoking instability that is not in the interests of India’s rulers, the Kashmiri people or the rest of South Asia. To avert these risks, it is vital that New Delhi devise an approach to address the wellsprings of public disaffection in the region. New Delhi should first and foremost seek to rebuild a basis of public trust in the region. That should begin with restoration of Jammu and Kashmir’s statehood, a step Prime Minister Modi himself has promised to take on several occasions. Though the move would be insufficient to quell all of Kashmiris’ grievances, it would at least remove one source of resentment. Making the chief minister subordinate to the New Delhi appointed lieutenant governor has been widely perceived as a humiliation. Reversing it would, to an extent, help win back Kashmir’s disillusioned pro-India political factions and could help weaken public sympathy for militancy. A decision on the issue nevertheless appears to have been delayed due to the government’s lack of confidence in security conditions following the Pahalgam attack. 114 The head BJP member of Jammu and Kashmir’s legislature said statehood will be restored when the security situation is under control. See “Statehood to J&K only after end to violence against youth, children: BJP’s Sunil Sharma”, PTI, 5 February 2026. More broadly, New Delhi prefers to maintain a firm grip on the region for a couple of reasons: it does not trust regional political forces to tackle militancy, and it seeks to build national political capital by proving it can control violence in Kashmir. Its current approach, however, is self-defeating. In the words of Chief Minister Omar Abdullah, there are “two parallel governments running the same territory”, with the lieutenant governor granted greater powers, especially in matters of public safety. 115 “ The Economic Times : ‘UT with an assembly is the worst form of government’: Omar Abdullah says two govts in J&K can’t work”, video, YouTube, 18 June 2025. Abdullah and other observers note that despite its prerogatives, the administration under the lieutenant governor lacks the grassroots networks needed to track militancy and prevent future attacks. 116 Crisis Group interviews, Srinagar, November 2025. See also “I take full responsibility: J&K LG Manoj Sinha calls Pahalgam attack a security failure”, Times of India , 14 July 2025. Restoring statehood would ... serve New Delhi’s longstanding goal of achieving greater participation by Kashmiris in India’s democracy. Restoring statehood would also serve New Delhi’s longstanding goal of achieving greater participation by Kashmiris in India’s democracy. For Kashmiris, the image of a disempowered government fosters the perception that voting in elections is futile. The two elections conducted after the change in the region’s status certainly recorded high voter turnout, with even separatists abstaining from their usual boycott calls. Even so, many voters cast their ballots to vent their frustration with New Delhi’s decisions and to keep the BJP at bay, rather than out of conviction that the outcome would make any material change. It was precisely disillusionment with Indian democracy that triggered the first major surge in militant violence in 1989. 117 New Delhi’s rigging of the 1987 regional polls was the trigger for the separatist insurgency that erupted in 1989, with many candidates who had been jailed turning to militancy upon their release. See Praveen Donthi, “ Kashmir Votes to Repudiate Rule from the Centre ”, Crisis Group Commentary, 14 October 2024. If restoring statehood is not feasible for political or security reasons in the short term, the central government should consider restoring some of the chief minister’s powers in the interim, with a degree of oversight by the lieutenant governor. The chief minister should, at the very least, have the power to appoint civil servants, one of the post’s main functions in all other Indian states and Union territories. The chief minister’s command of the police should also be restored, albeit by increments. Blocking the chief minister’s office from handling the threat of militancy is counterproductive, as security forces working alone cannot properly track local insurgent activity in a complex and evolving conflict. B. Loosening the Iron Grip The government’s determination to claim it has pacified Kashmir places immense pressure on security forces to live up to that expectation, resulting in the widespread use of draconian anti-terror laws against local people suspected of having militant links. But this approach has tended to fuel resentment of the Indian state, even spurring some of those marked for arrest to join or lend support to militant groups. 118 Crisis Group observations, Jammu and Kashmir, 2021-2025. See also “Youth share tales of harassment at PDP meet on why Kashmiri professionals are turning to violence”, The Hindu , 8 December 2025. Measures such as demolishing the homes of suspected militants’ families without investigation increase the collective sense of victimhood. So does dismissing government employees on mere suspicion of ties to insurgents. Given the consequences for those on the receiving end, New Delhi should stop applying its anti-terror laws so broadly. As an official admitted: “It’s better to make an example out of a handful of guilty people than to resort to collective punishment, which will backfire”. 119 Crisis Group interview, senior security official, Srinagar, 2024. Kashmiri observers have also voiced growing concern about rising radicalism and religious fundamentalism among the region’s young people, particularly among those arrested under the anti-terror laws who have come to embrace an extremist version of Islam as a way to cope with imprisonment. 120 Kashmiri observers point out that the government’s practice of transferring detained young Kashmiris to prisons outside the region, where most of the inmates are Hindu, is further pushing them to embrace religion. Crisis Group interview, Waheed Ur Rehman Para, member of Legislative Assembly, Srinagar, November 2025. The case of the young Kashmiri doctors who carried out the 2025 New Delhi blast suggests the problem extends beyond those in jail. 121 A Kashmiri legislator said the blast was not just a political act of terror but also had radical religious undertones. Crisis Group interview, Srinagar, November 2025. In private, security officials voice regret that New Delhi is solely focused on eliminating militants, while doing little to create conditions that discourage them or weaken their cause. 122 Crisis Group interview, senior security official, Kashmir, 2025. The use of harsh anti-terror laws for minor transgressions such as posts on social media stands out as particularly counterproductive, as does blacklisting young people who have been charged with disturbing law and order when they later apply for government jobs. 123 “J&K cops to deny security clearance to stone pelters for passport, govt jobs”, The Indian Express , 2 August 2021. C. India-Pakistan: Dialogue amid Distrust New Delhi shows little appetite for engagement with Islamabad given the terrorist attacks perpetrated on its territory, for which it has blamed its neighbour. While Islamabad has officially banned the jihadist groups Lashkar-e-Tayyeba and Jaish-e-Mohammad, which are allegedly responsible for many attacks, they have often re-emerged under changed names, including through charity and political fronts. While these too are proscribed, the groups still seem able to revive themselves, prompting New Delhi to accuse Pakistan of failing to take action against them. 124 Crisis Group Briefing, India-Pakistan: Avoiding a War in Waiting , op. cit. If it is to convince India that its efforts are genuine, Pakistan will need to aggressively enforce its ban on anti-Indian jihadist groups. India, for its part, should rethink its stance that Operation Sindoor has only been paused, as Modi has put it, implying that military action could immediately resume if another terrorist attack occurs. 125 Ibid. While this novel approach is meant to boost India’s deterrence, it puts India on a perpetual war footing and increases the risk of conflict with Pakistan, the consequences of which could be calamitous. 126 Ibid. Kashmiri militants, whether local or foreign, could well aim to conduct another terror attack on Indian soil. 127 The U.S. Directorate of National Intelligence assessed in its 2026 report that “conditions exist for terrorist actors to continue to create catalysts for crises”. See “Annual Threat Assessment of the US Intelligence Community”, Office of the Director of National Intelligence, March 2026, p. 24. For some observers, the next India-Pakistan conflict is thus “a question of when, not if”. 128 “In West Asia, a widening conflict with no clear ends”, Hindustan Times , 7 March 2026; “The faint hope for peace between India and Pakistan”, Time , 26 June 2026. It is true that, despite its combative posture and promises to retaliate against all attacks, the Indian government has proven more cautious than expected, taking great care not to blame Pakistan after the November 2025 New Delhi blast. But whether it can withstand domestic pressure in the event of another large-scale attack is hard to predict. In these circumstances, resuming a modicum of dialogue with Islamabad has taken on extra urgency. Insisting that Pakistan still backs anti-India jihadists, India has ... turned down Islamabad’s proposal of back-channel talks. New Delhi has thus far rebuffed Pakistan’s diplomatic overtures, including the Pakistani prime minister’s offer of dialogue to settle contentious issues, from terrorism to disputes over water sharing and the fate of Jammu and Kashmir. 129 Crisis Group Briefing, India-Pakistan: Avoiding a War in Waiting , op. cit. See also “PM urges India to ‘hold’ meaningful dialogue on Kashmir”, The News , 5 February 2025. Insisting that Pakistan still backs anti-India jihadists, India has also turned down Islamabad’s proposal of back-channel talks. 130 Maleeha Lodhi, “A year on, stalemate persists”, Dawn , 15 June 2026. The two sides have reportedly participated in a few discreet Track 1.5 and 2 dialogues, unofficial discussions held by former officials and experts who are not representatives of any state. 131 “India Pakistan held Track 1.5, 2 meetings after Operation Sindoor”, Hindustan Times , 17 April 2026. As a former senior Pakistani diplomat noted, however, such exchanges have limited value since participants seldom deviate from the stated positions of their home countries. 132 Lodhi, “A year on, stalemate persists”, op. cit. Signs of greater inclination to engage with Islamabad have nevertheless begun to emerge on the Indian side. A senior leader from the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS), the BJP’s powerful parent organisation, has for the first time spoken up about the need to engage with Pakistan, arguing that while India has every right to “respond appropriately” to terror incidents backed by Islamabad, it should leave the door to dialogue open. 133 “Why has the RSS called for dialogue with Pakistan?”, The Hindu , 17 May 2026; “‘India should not close doors for dialogue with Pakistan’: RSS general secretary Dattatreya Hosabale”, Times of India , 12 May 2026. Given the RSS’s influence, this stance could help assuage public hostility to diplomacy with Pakistan. 134 The Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (the National Volunteers Association, or RSS) is a Hindu nationalist organisation founded in 1925, of which the BJP is just one of many wings. With millions of members, it is considered the largest NGO in the world. For a critical view of the RSS, see “Mamdani opposes NYC event with leader of India’s Hindu nationalist group”, Reuters, 26 August 2026. Islamabad has reacted cautiously to the RSS call, with the foreign ministry waiting to see if its views reflect India’s official policy. 135 “FO waiting to see how India reacts to ‘pro-dialogue chorus”, Dawn , 15 May 2026. Few in Pakistan, however, are optimistic regarding the revival of formal talks with India so long as the BJP government continues to accuse the country of supporting jihadist groups and fighting a proxy war with its neighbour. 136 Crisis Group telephone interviews, August 2026. See also Touqir Hussain, “Modi’s Pakistan policy”, Dawn , 13 August 2026. Hussain is a former Pakistan ambassador. The absence of direct lines of communication beyond military-to-military channels increases conflict risks, including as the result of miscalculation or misunderstanding. Despite abiding distrust of its neighbour, India has, in the past, maintained communication through back channels with Pakistan, even in times of crisis. 137 The prime ministers of India and Pakistan spoke to each other even at the height of the Kargil conflict of 1999, for example, and the two national security advisers have been in regular touch during other tense episodes. At present, however, the only communication channel in place is a hotline between the directors general of military operations. Crisis Group Briefing, India-Pakistan: Avoiding a War in Waiting , op. cit. See also “India and Pakistan: Neighbours who do not talk to each other”, The India Forum , 10 April 2026. Since there are few prospects for formal talks between India and Pakistan’s top leaders, behind-the-scenes diplomacy could play a vital role in defusing the threat of fresh clashes. Such quiet contacts could enable political leaders to communicate, if not directly, then at least through their national security advisers. 138 Crisis Group Briefing, India-Pakistan: Avoiding a War in Waiting , op. cit. Reviving such a mechanism would allow both sides to communicate their red lines and, perhaps most importantly, avoid misunderstanding or misinterpretation of the other’s actions. They should establish this bilateral channel outside the limelight to avoid the domestic pressures both might face should news of it leak. At the same time, Indian authorities could make it clear to the public that any level of engagement would not amount to normalising relations or offering concessions to Islamabad, including over its territorial claims on Kashmir. Authorities in Islamabad could also assure the Pakistani public that Pakistan’s position on Kashmir’s disputed status or other contentious issues such as the country’s rights under the Indus Waters Treaty would not be compromised. Resuming quiet diplomacy would allow both [India and Pakistan] to share, examine and discuss their respective allegations outside the public eye. Even then, back-channel diplomacy is unlikely to make much headway if the Indian and Pakistani governments succumb to the temptation of nationalist outbursts and tit-for-tat allegations against each other. A tentative diplomatic opening is also likely to fail if Pakistan does not address India’s suspicions of continued support for anti-India jihadist groups more robustly. It is in Islamabad’s interest to rigorously enforce the law banning all jihadist entities. In return, Islamabad will expect New Delhi to respond to its concerns about alleged Indian backing for anti-Pakistan Baloch militant groups and the Pakistani Taliban. Progress in reducing mutual trust on such contentious issues is unlikely to happen overnight. But a high-level back channel between the national security advisers could still play an important role in this respect. Resuming quiet diplomacy would allow both to share, examine and discuss their respective allegations outside the public eye. Foreign governments that enjoy friendly relations with both parties, such as the U.S., the UK, EU member states, Saudi Arabia, Qatar, the United Arab Emirates and other Gulf countries, can also help stabilise the relationship. Considering India’s sensitivities regarding foreign interference or mediation on the Kashmir issue, external powers should move cautiously with quiet, behind-the-scenes diplomacy. They should emphasise that it is in New Delhi and Islamabad’s mutual interest to ensure a sustainable peace in South Asia, encouraging them to use high-level back channels to defuse potential conflict triggers. After seven years, the tough security measures and federal rule have not only failed to bring peace but may also have fostered support for militant groups in some circles. Srinagar, Kashmir, India. November 2025. CRISIS GROUP / Praveen Donthi VI. Conclusion Seven years after the Indian government revoked Jammu and Kashmir’s special autonomous status, redrew its boundaries, overhauled its administrative set-up and undertook numerous reforms ostensibly to foster peace, the threats to local and regional security from the restive Himalayan region persist – and have arguably grown more serious given their impact on relations with Pakistan. Though the government has succeeded in reducing conflict-related violence, the stringent measures it has employed to do so and the threat it has posed to Kashmiris’ sense of identity are fuelling deep discontent. New Delhi’s efforts to impose central rule appear not to have achieved their goal of eradicating militancy. They may even have fostered support in some circles for insurgent groups. If it is to achieve a durable peace in Jammu and Kashmir, India should address as a priority Kashmiris’ growing disaffection. Ideally, that would start by honouring the promise to restore the region’s statehood, paving the way to reinstatement of a democratically elected regional government with real power. New Delhi should also review its tactics in combating militant groups, particularly by being more discriminating in the way it applies its anti-terror laws. Sparked by a terrorist attack in Indian-administered Kashmir, the brief but intense clashes between India and Pakistan in 2025 were a stark reminder of how devastating this oft-forgotten dispute could be if it gets out of hand. Resumption of some form of dialogue between the two nuclear neighbours is essential, preferably through a discreet back channel. With its aspirations for a “New Kashmir” proving overly optimistic, the Indian government should do more to ensure that this unresolved conflict does not become the trigger for far greater harm. Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print 23 October 2026 CUBA The UN General Assembly will vote next week on its annual resolution condemning the U.S. embargo on Cuba, in place for more than six decades. Last year’s resolution passed 165-7. Washington is seeking to reduce the resolution’s backing as the Trump administration pursues a broader economic pressure campaign on the island (including restrictions on oil shipments and new secondary sanctions). U.S. Ambassador to the UN Mike Waltz hosted an event featuring Cuban dissidents, who argued that supporting the resolution excuses the Cuban government’s human rights abuses while obscuring its role in the country’s economic crisis. Cuban diplomats denounced the panel as an attempt to deflect attention from the embargo’s effects. Crisis Group expert Michael Bustamante says the confrontation illustrates the unfortunate either-or terms in which the debate is often framed. Decrying the humanitarian consequences of U.S. measures need not mean absolving the Cuban government of responsibility for its economic policy failures or its suppression of dissent. STRAIT OF HORMUZ October has already seen Iran hit more ships in or around the Strait of Hormuz than any previous month of the war that the U.S. and Israel launched in February. Tehran’s escalation comes after the volume of crude oil moving through the strait reached pre-war levels, largely through a scheme by which a few risk-tolerant tankers are assuming the danger of hauling barrels through the waterway before transferring their cargo to more risk-averse vessels outside it. Crisis Group expert Chris Newton says the question now is whether Iran can make these “shuttle runs” too costly. If it cannot, it will lose leverage in any negotiations with the U.S. and Gulf Arab countries that may transpire. But if it can, its attacks could prompt retaliatory U.S. strikes. U.S. - UKRAINE Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy announced on Tuesday that U.S. intelligence sharing, crucial for advance warning of incoming Russian ballistic missiles, had been restored. At the same time, there were conflicting reports on a slowdown in Ukraine’s access to the Starlink satellite system, which it depends on for battlefield communications and defensive drones. U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the “throttling” of Starlink, which is run by billionaire Elon Musk's company SpaceX, was a technical error that “no one ordered”. The incident nonetheless fuelled speculation that the Trump administration is scaling back intelligence and technological support for Ukraine to strong-arm Kyiv into making concessions to Moscow ahead of the 3 November U.S. midterm elections. Wednesday’s meeting between Trump’s envoy Steve Witkoff and Russian President Vladimir Putin, in which Witkoff called Putin a “humanitarian”, has done the same. Crisis Group expert Lucian Kim says Zelenskyy’s resistance to U.S. pressure has boosted his approval ratings at home. Polls show that a majority of Ukrainians oppose ceding territory in return for a peace settlement. 16 October 2026 IRAN Iranian attacks on shipping in and around the Strait of Hormuz have surged in October to date, with more than two dozen vessels struck since the month began. Meanwhile, Washington is maintaining its blockade of Iranian ports while backing oil shipments along the Omani coast, where smaller tankers transfer cargo to larger vessels outside the strait. Crisis Group expert Naysan Rafati says the uptick in Iranian strikes is an effort to counter a rebound in oil flows that showed Tehran’s grip on the Strait of Hormuz was weakening. Iran wants Washington to accept its proposed terms for a ceasefire that reopens the waterway in exchange for sanctions relief and an end to the U.S. blockade. But a diplomatic breakthrough appears less likely than the two sides setting off another escalatory spiral. SUDAN The Integrated Food Security Phase Classification, a UN-backed hunger monitor, warned Monday of growing famine risks in Sudan’s Darfur and Kordofan regions, driven by conflict, displacement and inadequate aid funding, and compounded by an El Niño-induced drought. This news comes as Sudan’s army reports advances against the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) in parts of North Kordofan and West Darfur. Meanwhile, the RSF continues to mount attacks in Blue Nile and to target El Obeid in North Kordofan with drones. Crisis Group expert Shewit Woldemichael says the army’s gains could make it more confident of victory, while continued RSF offensives suggest that this group, too, sees opportunities for battlefield gains. The continued fighting is likely to further complicate diplomatic efforts to end the war and ease Sudan’s humanitarian crisis. UKRAINE This past Sunday, U.S. President Donald Trump announced an “energy ceasefire” between Russia and Ukraine, saying each had agreed to halt attacks on the other’s energy infrastructure, following a deal he made to buy Russian diesel and ease related U.S. sanctions. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said he learned of the ceasefire through social media, adding that Washington threatened to suspend intelligence sharing unless Ukraine stopped striking Russian refineries. Ukrainian forces also reported restrictions on Starshield, the military version of SpaceX’s Starlink satellite service, which they depend on for communications and drone operations. Washington says it continues to share intelligence with Ukraine. Zelenskyy this week announced the resumption of refinery attacks as Russian strikes on Ukrainian energy infrastructure continued unabated. Crisis Group expert Lucian Kim says any disruption to intelligence or communications would compound Ukraine’s difficulties in protecting its cities and power grid as winter approaches, leaving civilians more vulnerable to prolonged heating and electricity outages. 9 October 2026 HAITI Haiti’s electoral council announced changes to the country’s voting rules Tuesday. The new law, which will likely result in delays to polls presently scheduled for 13 December, will remove provisions that would have disqualified individuals subject to bilateral sanctions imposed by third countries from running for office. U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio denied any U.S. involvement and said Washington would investigate the facts independently. Crisis Group expert Renata Segura says the incident comes amid already high tensions between Havana and Washington, after the U.S. halted fuel imports coming into Cuba, exacerbating a severe energy crisis on the island, in hopes of pushing the Cuban authorities to negotiate an economic and political opening. How Algeria’s Rupture with the UAE Could Roil the Region mloukili Fri, 10/23/2026 - 10:58 Latest Updates Africa Asia-Pacific Europe Latin America & Caribbean Middle East & North Africa United States Global Issues & Institutions My Reading List Algeria's President Abdelmadjid Tebboune (L) speaks with United Arab Emirates’ President Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan as they pose for a photo during the G7 Summit hosted by Italy, in Savelletri, on 14 June, 2024. AFP / Ludovic Marin Commentary / Middle East & North Africa 23 October 2026 13 minutes How Algeria’s Rupture with the UAE Could Roil the Region Algiers has severed diplomatic ties with Abu Dhabi, following years of discord over crises in North Africa and the Sahel. The two countries see their dispute very differently, but it has nonetheless become a rivalry that could put regional stability at risk. Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print Also available in Arabic English Arabic Michaël Béchir Ayari Senior Analyst, Tunisia Related Tags Algeria United Arab Emirates On 10 September, Algeria broke off diplomatic relations with the United Arab Emirates, in the latest manifestation of a confrontation between the two countries over policy in the Middle East, North Africa and the Sahel. Since 2020, disagreements have festered between Algiers and Abu Dhabi over Israel, Morocco and Western Sahara. Algeria has also grown increasingly suspicious of the aims of Emirati involvement in crises in Libya, Sudan and Sahelian states. The rupture is marked by an asymmetry of perceptions. Algiers sees the UAE, sitting far away in the Gulf, as interfering in its North African and Sahelian neighbourhood, where it is looking to rebuild the diplomatic clout that it wielded for decades after winning independence from French colonial rule in 1962. It views Emirati interventions as, at the very least, encroachments upon its historical domain. Abu Dhabi, for its part, says economic ties, not Algeria, are central to its African engagement. It forswears any intent to provoke or sideline Algiers. The bilateral discord has become a full-blown rivalry, however, and one that is becoming perilous as regional security arrangements are changing. Algeria is forging closer links with Niger, as well as with Chad. It is also backing the Sudanese army in its war with the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and Libya’s internationally recognised government in Tripoli in its power struggle with Field Marshal Khalifa Haftar, whose forces control the country’s east . Algerian officials describe these moves as reinforcing the country’s “ strategic borders ”. Algeria remains bitterly at odds with Morocco over Western Sahara and other issues, and it is just now repairing relations with Mali. Meanwhile, the UAE is forming its own partnerships in North Africa and the Sahel, which can involve both states and armed groups, and which often (though not always) put it indirectly in competition with Algeria. A direct clash between the two countries is unlikely. Their respective alliance systems overlap somewhat and do not constitute coherent groups of adversaries. Still, jostling among them could draw in Algeria, the UAE or both, with the risk of local escalation or inadvertent confrontation. Roots of the Break-up Dramatic as the 10 September rupture was, it had been a long time coming. Until 2020, relations between Algeria and the UAE were strong. In the early 1970s, Algeria sent oil experts, including executives from Sonatrach, Algeria’s state-owned hydrocarbons company, to the Gulf to help establish the institutions that would become the Abu Dhabi National Oil Company. Abdelaziz Bouteflika, who served as Algeria’s president between 1999 and 2019, lived in Abu Dhabi from 1984 to 1987, working as a diplomatic adviser to Sheikh Zayed bin Sultan Al Nahyan, father of today’s leader Mohammed bin Zayed (aka MBZ). During Bouteflika’s tenure as Algerian head of state, Emirati capital made significant inroads into the Algerian economy, including in the defence sector. In 2012, for example, Emirati investors cooperated with the Algerian defence ministry and state-owned companies in joint ventures to produce Mercedes-Benz vehicles and Emirati-designed NIMR armoured vehicles in Algeria. The UAE built networks of contacts within the Algerian political, business and military elite, some of which survived Bouteflika’s fall in 2019. The UAE’s 2020 normalisation with Israel – part of what is known as the Abraham Accords – opened a first crack in the relationship. Algiers firmly opposed any Arab state forging ties with Israel before a comprehensive settlement of the Israeli-Palestinian conflict. In September 2020, President Abdelmadjid Tebboune criticised what he described as a “ rush ” ( empressement ) toward normalisation, declaring that Algeria would not be part of it. Algiers has long been the foremost outside backer of the Polisario Front, the group battling for an independent Western Sahara. Algerian concerns grew further when, on 4 November 2020, the UAE became the first Arab country to open a consulate in Western Sahara, establishing a diplomatic office in Laayoune, a city in the Moroccan-controlled part of the disputed territory. Algiers has long been the foremost outside backer of the Polisario Front, the group battling for an independent Western Sahara. Sabri Boukadoum, then Algeria’s foreign minister, questioned the move’s compatibility with international law and reaffirmed Algerian support for Sahrawi self-determination. A month later, Morocco followed the UAE in normalising relations with Israel, prompting Algerian authorities to discern an emerging UAE-Morocco-Israel alliance in their immediate vicinity. This perception was significantly reinforced in November 2021, when Morocco and Israel signed a landmark defence cooperation agreement . The agreement formalised defence ties and paved the way for cooperation in areas including intelligence and military training. Algerian authorities viewed this deepening partnership as tantamount to a direct threat , part of a regional alignment aimed at weakening their country. Algerian worries extended to allegations of foreign interference in domestic affairs. Officials accused Morocco and Israel of supporting the Movement for the Self-Determination of Kabylia (MAK) , an independence movement that Algeria designated a terrorist organisation in 2021. As evidence, they pointed to the fact that Morocco’s representative at the UN had publicly argued that the Kabyle people are entitled to exercise a right to self-determination . A number of former Algerian diplomats and commentators implicated the UAE in these purported destabilisation efforts as well: a Morocco-based think-tank separately reported on contacts between MAK representatives and Emirati figures, citing sources within the Kabyle independence movement, among others. The Dispute Deepens Other regional disagreements added to the tensions. In 2020 and again in 2022 , Abu Dhabi opposed the appointment of successive Algerian foreign ministers as UN envoys to Libya, against the backdrop of Emirati support for Field Marshal Haftar, and Algeria’s closer links with the authorities in Tripoli. The UAE cited the objections of Arab states and Libyan actors, expressing their concern that Algeria, as a neighbouring country deeply involved in the conflict, could not be viewed as an impartial mediator. Another friction point surfaced in 2023, when Algerian government-aligned media attributed the failure of Algeria’s BRICS application to Emirati manoeuvring against its candidacy. Views in Algiers on how to counter the UAE’s gambits – real and perceived – may not have been entirely aligned. Some elements of the security establishment and associated media favoured a confrontational approach, while others, including figures close to former army Chief of Staff Ahmed Gaïd Salah, worried about jeopardising significant economic interests and longstanding personal connections. The exact boundaries of these contrasting viewpoints, however, remained unclear. As Emirati actions increasingly clashed with Algeria’s regional priorities and came to be perceived as national security threats , displaying restraint became more difficult. Despite his initial reticence to comment on the matter, President Tebboune’s criticism of the UAE gradually became louder. Despite his initial reticence to comment on the matter, President Tebboune’s criticism of the UAE gradually became louder. In 2024, he complained that wherever conflict erupted in the region , the money of an unnamed Gulf state could be found behind it; in 2025, he said Algeria enjoyed good relations with all Gulf monarchies, except one . By the following February, he was openly denouncing a “ mini-state ” that was destabilising the Arab world and the Sahel. Successive attempts to ease tensions made little headway. Former Algerian diplomats told Crisis Group that Gulf states, including Bahrain and Oman, sent emissaries to Algiers to try mediating between the two sides. They said Algeria rejected these efforts, however, and will keep doing so as long as what it regards as Emirati meddling continues. Direct contacts endured, but they failed to achieve a thaw. By February, when Algeria terminated the 2013 bilateral agreement that provided the legal framework for air travel between the two countries, the room for compromise had considerably narrowed. Rivalry in the Sahel As relations deteriorated, the dispute increasingly spilled into a contest for influence in North Africa and the Sahel. A May 2024 tour of Mali, Niger and Burkina Faso by UAE Minister of State Sheikh Shakhboot bin Nahyan Al Nahyan raised hackles in Algeria , which has long described Mali in particular as a “brother” nation. Abu Dhabi was offering the Sahelian capitals cooperation on counter-terrorism just as Western influence was waning in the region and the new Alliance of Sahel States (AES) was opening it to new external patrons. There were other angles as well: for the UAE, security cooperation is inseparable from economic interests, particularly when it comes to natural resources; Dubai’s role in the international gold trade, including gold originating in the Sahel, gave the UAE an additional stake in regional developments. Meanwhile, Algeria’s historical ties with Bamako and the other AES capitals were reaching a nadir. Emirati officials maintain that its engagement was not aimed at supplanting Algeria. Indeed, they rarely present Algiers as a competitor when discussing the Sahel or any other African region. Rather, they say, Abu Dhabi is pursuing a broad strategy, rooted in geo-economics , designed to expand the UAE’s footprint on a continent that has gained in importance. As an Emirati businessman and former government official told Crisis Group in explaining the scope of Abu Dhabi’s ambition, “You’re either at the table or on the menu”. Algerian officials, by contrast, view the UAE’s combination of investments and partnerships with governments, business elites and armed actors as a means of undermining their country’s interests. They regard the Sahel as crucial to Algerian security, particularly since Bamako abandoned the Algeria-mediated 2015 peace agreement with armed separatists in northern Mali, whom they fear could make common cause with co-ethnics on the Algerian side of the border. Algerian concerns were heightened by allegations of ransom payments , mentioned in an August UN report and linked to the UAE by regional sources , to the jihadist group JNIM that has grabbed chunks of Malian and other Sahelian state territory. Algiers has long argued that such payments strengthen armed groups active near its frontiers. The contrast in approach and threat perceptions became particularly acute over events in Niger. Following a 2023 coup there, relations between Algiers and Niamey soured, and they worsened further in April 2025, when Niger recalled its ambassador from Algiers in solidarity with authorities in Bamako, with whom Algiers was then at loggerheads over the abrogated peace agreement and other issues. Bilateral ties subsequently improved, following Nigerien leader General Abdourahamane Tiani’s visit to Algiers the following February . The two countries revived their security cooperation, and Niger even helped broker the present rapprochement between Algeria and Mali. Relations with Niger ... have an important economic dimension for both Algeria and the UAE. Relations with Niger also have an important economic dimension for both Algeria and the UAE. Algeria considers Niger key to its effort to reconnect with sub-Saharan Africa through energy and trade. Its flagship project is the Trans-Saharan Gas Pipeline , intended to carry Nigerian gas through Niger into Algeria and onward to Europe. Here, the UAE has a competing interest: the Trans-Saharan route directly competes with Morocco’s Atlantic pipeline , which is expected to run along the West African coast and which the UAE has backed with early financing. It is against this backdrop that Algeria viewed a failed coup against Tiani on 29 August as threatening its interests. Rumours swirled in Algiers about an Emirati hand . To date, these are unsubstantiated, but they have only deepened suspicions regarding the UAE’s activities in the Sahel. Algeria responded to the coup attempt by deploying four Su-30MKA fighter jets to Niamey , accompanied by an Il-78 aerial-refuelling aircraft and an Il-76 transport plane. Algerian analysts told Crisis Group that mechanics, logistics specialists and personnel for force protection were also dispatched. Beyond sending a clear signal of support for Tiani’s government, these steps showcased Algeria’s determination to regain influence in a region where it has lost considerable ground – and where it appears to have identified the UAE as a chief antagonist. Algeria’s actions also embodied something more, again with implications for relations with the UAE: a shift away from its longstanding aversion to military operations abroad. Since independence, Algeria’s leaders have framed the country’s foreign policy around non-alignment, anti-imperialism, national sovereignty, diplomatic mediation, South-South solidarity, support for national liberation and self-determination movements, and, importantly, non-interference in other states’ domestic affairs. There have been exceptions, and Algeria has at times interpreted this last precept flexibly when it has felt that it has important interests at stake. Overall, however, reluctance to dispatch regular military forces abroad has remained a powerful institutional constraint. Only in 2020 did a constitutional amendment create a legal framework for overseas deployments. The latter still require parliamentary approval and are restricted to internationally sanctioned missions. More recently, the army’s top general Saïd Chengriha has promoted the concept that Algeria has “ strategic borders ”. Though it does not formally establish a right to military intervention in neighbouring countries, this notion expands Algeria’s security perimeter by treating instability, armed groups and trafficking networks beyond its frontiers as potential national security threats. Rivalry in North Africa and the Horn In other regional conflicts, Algeria and the UAE likewise stand on opposing sides. In Libya, Field Marshal Haftar’s forces have, over time, received extensive Emirati backing . In contrast, Algeria has stood with Tripoli (which itself has maintained tight relations with Niger). In Sudan, Algeria sides with the army, whose leaders it considers the country’s legitimate representatives; several Algerian analysts told Crisis Group that in 2025 Algiers discreetly provided the Sudanese army with equipment, including old Russian MiG-29 fighter jets and spare parts. By contrast, Abu Dhabi refers to the army-led administration as the “ Port Sudan authority ”, in reference to its erstwhile seat in Port Sudan, treating it merely as one party to the conflict; it is widely believed to be sending support to the army’s main adversary, the RSF, though the UAE denies the claim. The divergent policies toward Sudan have had wider repercussions. Eastern and southern Libya reportedly have served as logistical corridors for supplies to the RSF allegedly originating with the Emirates . Previously, much of this materiel allegedly went through eastern Chad. For its part, the UAE maintains that its activities in eastern Chad are humanitarian , particularly getting aid to Sudanese refugees. An Algerian expert told Crisis Group that policymakers in Algiers appear intent on deepening ties with N’Djamena at least in part to counterbalance what they view as Sudan-linked Emirati networks in Chad. That said, Chadian President Idriss Déby has invested considerable political capital in his relationship with the UAE, whose substantial financial support , including a $1.5 billion budget financing agreement signed in 2023, gives the latter sway that Algeria would struggle to match. The growing Algeria-UAE rivalry could deepen existing Libyan divisions and turn local disputes into arenas of indirect regional confrontation. These competing relationships run the risk of reinforcing regional divisions, with Field Marshal Haftar and Chad being generally close to Abu Dhabi, while Tripoli and Niger cooperate more with Algiers. Conversely, the growing Algeria-UAE rivalry could deepen existing Libyan divisions and turn local disputes into arenas of indirect regional confrontation. To some extent, it already has. In August 2024, for example, Haftar’s forces moved toward Ghadames, only a few kilometres from the Algerian frontier, a development Algiers saw as threatening. The crisis eventually subsided after Haftar’s spokesman denied that the city was a military objective and insisted that the border with Algeria was secure . Still, the episode reinforced perceptions in Algiers of a UAE-backed menace in its neighbourhood. Tensions continue to build. Algeria is increasingly concerned by Haftar’s influence in southern Libya, where his forces have tightened their grip on lucrative trafficking routes and strengthened cooperation with N’Djamena in fighting Chadian rebel groups. Haftar has thus obtained access to an important source of income and displaced Chadian rebels toward northern Niger, particularly the strategic Salvador Pass area , exacerbating instability near Algeria’s southern border. All in all, these developments help explain Algeria’s evolving approach to regional security. Rather than viewing events in Libya, Niger and Sudan separately, Algiers increasingly sees them as interconnected challenges. Containing the Clash What began as a downturn in Algerian-UAE relations has thus evolved into a full-blown crisis with possible reverberations across the northern third of Africa. Algeria has remained silent as to why precisely it severed diplomatic ties. The foreign ministry’s statement was vague , referring to “provocative or hostile” actions as well as warnings that had failed to deter Abu Dhabi from unspecified behaviour. Algeria may have avoided identifying grievances or conditions for reconciliation in order to allow for flexibility in future talks. The difficulty of substantiating its complaints may also have contributed to its ambiguous stance. To officials in Abu Dhabi, the break was both unanticipated and perplexing. Though he did not name Algeria, Anwar Gargash, a diplomatic adviser to the UAE president, alluded to it in a tweet complaining of “ puzzles and signals that require decoding ” in interstate relations. The UAE foreign ministry adopted a more conciliatory tone, expressing hope that the rupture would prove temporary. A number of Emirati analysts said the dispute is of far greater significance to Algeria than to the UAE, given Abu Dhabi’s preoccupation with the war in the Gulf. These reactions underscore a divergence in perspectives: while Algiers views Abu Dhabi’s alliances as a growing threat to its regional influence, Abu Dhabi sees its engagement as part of a strategy driven by political, economic and security interests that go beyond any bilateral relationship. In reality, neither country can bar the other from an ever more cutthroat arena. Too, governments and armed groups in the region cannot be neatly categorised into two rival blocs; each of Niger, Chad and the assorted Libyan players has its own agenda that may not align precisely with either Algerian or Emirati wishes. Still, as Algeria assumes a more assertive stance and the UAE pursues its geographically expansive approach, seemingly oblivious to, or at least underestimating the depth of Algeria’s concerns and its conviction that Abu Dhabi is challenging its position, bilateral tensions risk becoming more fraught. Informal communication channels could help shed light on their respective intentions and minimise the chance of misinterpretation and accidental conflict. The two countries would be far better served by taking steps and shifting their mindsets to help ensure that Emirati influence in Algeria’s neighbourhood, and Algiers’ response to it, do not become a trigger for bilateral confrontation. First, though full reconciliation may be out of reach for the moment, maintaining or restoring informal communication channels could help shed light on their respective intentions and minimise the chance of misinterpretation and accidental conflict. Secondly, Algiers should avoid construing every Emirati undertaking in neighbouring countries as part of a strategy directed against its interests. Finally, Abu Dhabi ought to take Algeria’s security concerns more seriously. It should recognise that its regional partnerships, particularly those involving armed non-state actors, may threaten Algerian interests, even when not so intended. Both countries should have an interest in preventing local disputes from drawing them further toward confrontation, particularly given that both neighbouring governments and armed groups pursue agendas neither side can fully control. Absent such efforts, the rift could deepen, increasing the risk that local crises spiral into open hostility. The result would be to exacerbate tensions in a region already riven by deadly conflict. Yemen: Houthi Attack on Taizz Road Threatens Lives, Welfare. Click to expand Image The Hayjat al-Abd road, which connects Aden to Taizz city, Yemen, September 26, 2026. © 2026 Photo by AFP via Getty Images (Beirut) – The Houthi armed group on October 18, 2026, used explosives to severely damage a critical road into Yemen’s besieged city of Taizz, putting civilian lives and welfare at increased risk, Human Rights Watch said today. The Hayjat al-Abd road has been the main entry point for food, medicine, and fuel to reach residents of Taizz city, which the Houthis have besieged since 2015. Fighting in the area has primarily been between the Houthis and forces aligned with Yemen’s internationally recognized government. The Houthis’ deliberate destruction of segments of the road, if intended to disable infrastructure indispensable to civilian survival, would violate the laws of war and amount to a war crime. The attack may also have caused disproportionate civilian harm. “The Houthi attack on the remaining commercial supply route to besieged Taizz further endangers civilians already struggling with severe shortages of food, water, medicine, and fuel,” said Niku Jafarnia, Yemen and Bahrain researcher at Human Rights Watch. “If Taizz residents’ access along this vital route is cut off for a prolonged period, they could face even greater risks to their lives and well-being.” Human Rights Watch spoke to eight informed sources in October about two attacks on the road and their aftermath, including civil society workers and a relative of a witness to the October 18 attack. Human Rights Watch also analyzed satellite imagery and verified photographs and a video from sources or posted on social media. In 2024, Human Rights Watch spoke with six Taizz residents about the difficulty of meeting basic needs during the Houthi siege. Human Rights Watch wrote to the Houthis on October 21 about attacks on the road but did not receive a response. Control over Taizz has been divided since 2015, when Houthi forces entered the governorate and surrounded its capital, Taizz city, Yemen’s third largest city. The city has remained under Yemeni government control, but the Houthis have cut off vital roads connecting it to the rest of the country, notably the port city of Aden, the Yemeni government’s current capital. While the laws of war do not prohibit sieges directed at military objectives, besieging forces are prohibited from using starvation of civilians as a method of warfare and must allow and facilitate humanitarian relief. Human Rights Watch has found that the Houthis’ blocking of roads into Taizz has severely restricted civilians’ ability to move in and out of the city and impeded the flow of essential goods, including water, and humanitarian access to the civilian population. Click to expand Image Graphic © 2026 Human Rights Watch At about 4:00 a.m. on October 18, Houthi forces detonated explosives on the Hayjat al-Abd road in the town of al-Turba, significantly damaging a portion of the road. Residents in the area as well as two other informed sources said that the Houthis had been in control of al-Turba, about 75 kilometers south of Taizz city, since October 4. Since then, there had been no ground fighting in the area, including on the night of the attack. Nor had there been any indications that government forces or other armed groups were trying to re-enter the area, indicating that there was not another group that could have carried out the attack. Another source said his relative told him: “It was a massive and terrifying explosion—everyone woke up. Rocks reached all the way to my house.” Human Rights Watch verified and geolocated four photographs and a video from sources showing a damaged culvert on the switchbacks of the Hayjat al-Abd road. The damage is consistent with a subsurface detonation of explosives. Two weeks earlier, apparent Houthi forces had attacked the Hayjat al-Abd road about 85 kilometers southeast of Taizz city. A civil society worker in Taizz who spoke with several people knowledgeable about the attack said that on the night and early morning of September 30-October 1, Houthi forces and Yemeni government-aligned forces fought on several fronts around Taizz. The sources said that Houthi forces infiltrated and reached the Hayjat al-Abd road, placing and detonating explosives in a culvert under the road just past Souq al-Wahati, a local market. The Houthi forces then withdrew. Two other sources gave similar accounts based on communications with local residents. Human Rights Watch was unable to conclusively determine that Houthi forces carried out the attack. Human Rights Watch verified and geolocated two additional photographs posted on social media on October 1 showing a damaged culvert on the Hayjat al-Abd road at the village of al-Muharraqah, where the road starts ascending to Taizz city. The damage to the culvert in the images is consistent with a subsurface detonation of explosives. Satellite imagery captured at 6:57 a.m. on October 1 shows damage to the culvert across the full width of the road. Government forces quickly retook the area after the first attack and later filled the destroyed portion of the road with dirt to allow vehicles to cross. Two sources said that government authorities had largely closed down the road to avoid further attacks on vehicles, though some vehicles continued to pass through. Since the October 1 attack, all roads into and out of Taizz have largely been blocked by Yemeni government-affiliated and Houthi forces due to hostilities. However, before the second attack, some supplies, including flour, had still been taken to Taizz city on the Hayjat al-Abd road, said two civil society workers in the area. However, the United Nations World Food Programme (WFP) said on October 14 that they had not been able to access the “more than 600,000 people in Taiz who depend on humanitarian assistance,” which was “especially alarming” since most of Taizz’s districts are considered to have emergency levels of hunger. The WFP also said that “wheat flour stocks are nearly exhausted” in the city and that “remaining food supplies in local markets may last only a short time if access constraints continue.” Under international humanitarian law, roads are presumptively civilian objects that become military objectives if by their nature, location, purpose, or use, they make an effective contribution to military action and their destruction, capture, or neutralization provides a definite military advantage at the time. Even if the Hayjat al-Abd road qualifies as a military objective, an attack would be unlawfully disproportionate if the expected incidental civilian harm would be excessive in relation to the concrete and direct military advantage anticipated. Given the road’s critical role in Taizz city civilians’ access to food, water, medicine, and other basic needs, the assessment should account for the reasonably foreseeable consequences of damaging or closing it. The Houthis should have known, particularly given the UN’s repeated warnings, that supplies in Taizz were running out and that further closures after October 1 from attacks on the road could have grave effects for besieged Taizz civilians relying on the road for necessities. International humanitarian law also prohibits attacking, destroying, or rendering useless objects indispensable to the survival of a civilian population. The October 18 attack disrupted the remaining major commercial supply route to Taizz city.
