Whether it violated this prohibition depends on whether it was carried out for the purpose of denying civilians access to objects indispensable to their survival. Serious violations of the laws of war ordered or committed with criminal intent—that is, deliberately or recklessly—are war crimes. “The fighting in Taizz could have dire consequences for the hundreds of thousands of civilians in need of aid,” Jafarnia said. “All warring parties should take care to protect civilians in Yemen who have already experienced considerable suffering over 12 years of conflict.”

Egypt: Drop Charges Against Prominent Journalist. Click to expand Image Lina Attalah, editor-in-chief of Mada Masr, in Cairo, Egypt, November 24, 2017. © 2017 Roger Anis/AP Photo Update October 28, 2026: On October 27, 2026, the New Cairo Misdemeanor Court convicted Lina Attalah after just one session, fined her 3 million Egyptian pounds (US$53,474) and ordered the website’s closure. Authorities took Attalah into custody after the hearing before releasing her hours later following payment of the fine. (Beirut) – Egyptian authorities should drop their case against Lina Attalah, editor-in-chief of the independent media outlet Mada Masr, ahead of her October 27, 2026 hearing, Human Rights Watch said today. The Supreme State Security Prosecution (SSSP) referred Attalah for trial on October 22 in Case No. 9072/2026 on charges of establishing and managing a website without a license. The referral came the day after prosecutors questioned her over the outlet’s reporting. She faces a fine of up to 3 million Egyptian pounds (about US$53,400) as well as the closure of Mada Masr and confiscation of its equipment. “The hasty prosecution of Lina Attalah marks another escalation in Egyptian authorities’ outrageous attack on independent media in the country,” said Bassam Khawaja, deputy Middle East and North Africa director at Human Rights Watch. “No journalist should face criminal prosecution for doing their job.” On October 19, prosecutors summoned Attalah for questioning. On October 21, they questioned Attalah over allegations of publishing “false news” and operating a website without a license, then released her on bail of 100,000 Egyptian pounds (about $1,780). The following day, prosecutors referred her for trial on charges of operating the website without a license. According to Mada Masr, this is the sixth case brought against the outlet or its journalists in the past six years. Egypt’s 2018 Press and Media Regulation Law requires websites operating in Egypt to obtain a license from the Supreme Council for Media Regulation. The law allows the council to suspend or block websites operating without a valid license. Mada Masr reported that it applied for a license in 2018 and again in 2020. It said that the authorities rejected its application without notifying it and that the platform had challenged that rejection in court. In 2023, Mada Masr submitted a new application with additional documents, and the authorities have not yet responded. Attalah’s prosecution raises concerns about the use of licensing requirements to restrict independent media, Human Rights Watch said. Arbitrary licensing rejections or weaponizing licensing requirements by failing to respond promptly to good faith efforts to comply and forcing entities into legal limbo violates international human rights law. Egyptian authorities have repeatedly targeted Attalah and Mada Masr. In September 2022, prosecutors questioned Attalah and three Mada Masr journalists over allegations of publishing false news, disturbing public peace, and harming public interest. In November 2023, prosecutors summoned Attalah for questioning following an investigation by the Supreme Council for Media Regulation. In August 2025, prosecutors again questioned Attalah over allegations of publishing “false news” and operating a website without a license, following Mada Masr’s reporting on alleged abuses at Badr 3 prison. More than a hundred civil society organizations, including Human Rights Watch, have called on Egyptian authorities to end the prosecution of Attalah and grant Mada Masr a license to operate. Attalah’s prosecution comes amid a broader crackdown on independent media in Egypt and less than a month after security forces arrested six journalists working for the independent investigative journalism platform Matsda2sh on September 28 and 29, 2026. The journalists, who constituted the platform’s entire editorial newsroom, remain in pretrial detention facing charges of “joining and financing a terrorist group,” “spreading false news,” and using social media to disseminate it. Some of them have since alleged that the authorities tortured them in detention and attempted to extract coerced confessions, according to their lawyers. The authorities should drop all charges stemming from exercising the right to freedom of expression and end their repeated harassment of independent media, Human Rights Watch said. Egypt remains one of the world’s leading jailers of journalists, with 25 journalists behind bars as of early October, according to the Committee to Protect Journalists. Egyptian authorities have blocked access to Mada Masr’s website in Egypt since May 2017. Egypt is obligated under the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights and the African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights to respect freedom of expression, including press freedom. The United Nations Human Rights Committee, which authoritatively interprets the covenant, has found that governments may not prohibit a site or an information dissemination system from publishing material solely on the basis that it may be critical of the government. “Setting registration requirements and then repeatedly ignoring Mada Masr’s good faith attempts to fulfill them is a transparent attempt by authorities to undermine the platform and violates international human rights law,” Khawaja said. “The Egyptian authorities should drop the charges and end the ongoing crackdown on independent journalism.”

Azerbaijan’s Hijab Restrictions Exclude Girls From School. Click to expand Image Three Azerbaijani women wearing headscarves in Baku, Azerbaijan. © 2019 Getty Images School officials across Azerbaijan have been turning away girls wearing hijabs following the introduction of new government dress regulations, sparking protests across the country. Police have detained dozens of people amid the protests, while Instagram and TikTok users have reported difficulties accessing the platforms as public criticism of the restrictions has grown. Azerbaijan’s Cabinet of Ministers amended school uniform regulations on September 21, prohibiting clothing "inconsistent with the principle of secular education." Although the regulations do not explicitly mention hijabs, schools began refusing entry to girls wearing headscarfs when the rules took effect on October 12. News reports showed distressed girls after being turned away from schools. Separate dress requirements adopted on October 6 also affected teachers. Authorities responded to the protests with widespread detentions. The Ministry of Interior acknowledged on October 12 that they had detained 37 people in Baku, alleging disruptions to public order. Independent media reported that more than 200 people were detained near a central Baku metro station that evening. Activists also reported 88 detentions in Nardaran village, with criminal cases opened against many of those detained. People criticizing the restrictions online have also faced detention. Unidentified individuals reportedly took activist İlkin Hüseynov from his home on October 14, a day after he launched "Let Leyli Go to School," an online initiative connecting volunteer teachers with girls excluded from classrooms. He was subsequently sentenced to 30 days detention for allegedly disobeying police orders. In Nakhchivan, a man reportedly received a sentence for 25 days detention following a TikTok post about the restrictions. Social media users across Azerbaijan also reported difficulties accessing Instagram and TikTok on October 12; some were only able to connect via virtual private networks. Excluding girls from schools because they wear religious headscarves interferes with their rights to education and freedom of religion or belief, and raises serious concerns about discrimination. While governments may regulate school attire, any restrictions must be lawful, necessary, proportionate and non-discriminatory. Azerbaijan should not use the principle of secular education to deny girls access to schooling. Azerbaijani authorities should immediately ensure that students and teachers wearing hijabs can attend schools, release anyone detained solely for peacefully protesting or criticizing the restrictions, ensure access to legal counsel for those in custody, and investigate reports of interference with social media access.

Egypt: Prominent Journalist Lina Attalah Detained. Click to expand Image Lina Attalah, editor-in-chief of Mada Masr, in Cairo, Egypt, November 24, 2017. © 2017 Roger Anis/AP Photo (Beirut) - The New Cairo Misdemeanor Court convicted Lina Attalah, editor-in-chief of the independent news platform Mada Masr, of operating without a license in a single hearing on October 27, 2026. The court fined her 3 million Egyptian pounds (US$53,474) and ordered the website’s closure. The authorities took Attalah into custody after the hearing. Mada Masr reported that prior to ruling, the judge cleared the courtroom, rejected all procedural motions presented by Attalah’s defense team including requests to present evidence and hear from witnesses, and replaced her defense counsel against her will. Attalah had received a summons on October 19 to appear for questioning before the Supreme State Security Prosecution and Egyptian authorities on October 22 referred her to trial on charges of establishing, managing, and operating a website without a license. The following quote can be attributed to Bassam Khawaja, deputy Middle East and North Africa director at Human Rights Watch: “The summary conviction of Lina Attalah in a sham process involving a single, rushed hearing is a complete travesty of justice. President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi’s government is clearly determined to wipe out the last remnants of independent media in the country. Egypt’s international partners should loudly condemn this outrageous crackdown.”

Syria's New Reconstruction Fund a Chance for Reform. Click to expand Image An aerial view of a damaged area of Damascus where the debris from collapsed buildings is being turned into sand, gravel, and bricks to reuse as construction materials to restore areas affected by Syria’s civil war, November 2, 2025. © 2025 Bakr Al Kasem/Anadolu via Getty Images Syria and the World Bank Group announced on October 18 the creation of the Syria Recovery and Reconstruction Trust Fund, known as START. Run by the World Bank, the fund will pool donor money and private investment to help restore infrastructure and public services, strengthen state institutions, and finance reforms the Syrian government identifies as priorities. The World Bank estimates Syria’s post-conflict reconstruction will cost about US$216 billion. Norway pledged approximately 90 million krone ($9.6 million) and the Netherlands €15 million ($16.8 million). START’s initial focus, according to Syria’s state news agency, SANA, is infrastructure, health and education. It will operate under World Bank policies, which include standards on stakeholder engagement, land acquisition, and grievance mechanisms. But those standards only cover START-funded projects and governance arrangements are still being finalized, according to SANA. The moment offers a chance to strengthen protections for Syria’s wider reconstruction, beyond START’s projects. Current rules governing reconstruction do not require consultation with affected communities, including tenants, informal occupants, and displaced people before projects are approved, and there is no specialized mechanism for reconstruction disputes. The consequences of policies that are implemented without consulting those most affected are already evident: In March, local authorities in Damascus proposed giving foreign companies land in Jobar and Qaboun in exchange for financing and building a reconstruction project. Owners of homes in zoned areas would get new units half the size of their old ones. Owners of land in informal settlements would get only 30 percent of their land. And the plan made no provision for tenants. The World Bank and START's donors should make a rights-aligned framework for housing, land, and property a priority among the reforms the fund supports, including an independent property dispute mechanism. They should require human rights impact assessments before funding projects with unresolved property claims. They should prioritize restoring services where people are returning. And any support for private health or education providers should carry enforceable requirements on affordability, quality, and nondiscrimination. Finance Minister Yisr Barnieh says the priority now is “tangible results for the Syrian people.” The real test is whether those people have a say in decisions about their land and whether they can enjoy their rights to health, education, and housing.

Brazil: New Evidence of Serious Police Misconduct in Deadly Raid. Play Video Read a text description of this video TEXT ON SCREEN October 28, 2025 Rio de Janeiro, Brazil NARRATION On the morning of October 28th, 2025, hundreds of police officers surrounded two low-income neighborhoods in Rio de Janeiro. By nightfall, the operation would become the deadliest in Brazil's history. TEXT ON SCREEN WARNING. This video contains graphic content, including blurred images of dead bodies. Viewer discretion advised. NARRATION 122 people were killed, including two children and five police officers. According to the autopsy records, over eighty five percent of non-police victims were Black. Police in Rio de Janeiro are required by Supreme Court order to wear body cameras. However, only twenty-three percent of officers wore body cameras that day, and in the footage reviewed by Human Rights Watch, not a single killing was captured on camera. LOWER THIRD Damir Khairat Research Technologist Digital Investigations Lab NARRATION Human Rights Watch was given access to the prosecutor's investigation into the operation, including 8,800 pages of records, 122 autopsies, and nearly 4,000 hours of body camera footage. TEXT ON SCREEN Prosecutors have released the body camera footage shown in this video. Most footage is sealed as evidence and cannot be published. NARRATION Watching all the footage day and night without any breaks would have taken a single researcher almost six months. So, we trained several artificial intelligence models to help us identify the moments that mattered most. First, we needed to organize everything. The models, alongside software that Human Rights Watch developed, synchronized recordings from different officers, mapped their locations, and scanned footage for gunshots and signs of camera tampering. From there we had a searchable platform that let us view the operation as one coordinated event, rather than thousands of separate recordings. What we found was evidence of widespread tampering and obstruction of body cameras. And it consistently happened at the exact moment cameras should have been recording, during arrests, shootouts, or while officers entered homes. Authorities said that the purpose of the raid was to arrest suspected drug traffickers. The evidence we found points to an operation that appeared lethal by design. To explain how we came to this conclusion, let's look at some examples of the moments we trained our AI models to detect. An officer's camera captured this video in an alleyway as a large group of his colleagues pass by, after which the officer quickly covers his camera. He or another officer then flags that there's a camera recording. SOUNDBITE [IN PORTUGUESE] The team has a camera. The team has a camera. No, no I’m talking about the thing there. NARRATION It's unclear why he covered it, but prosecutors later charged him with camera tampering. SOUNDBITE So, this would be the kind of like overall operational view. NARRATION To find incidents like this across almost 4,000 hours of footage from nearly 500 officers, we trained a model to detect similar moments when a camera continued recording, but the lens was covered. Here, an officer is seen struggling to pick the lock on the door of someone's home. Once it's open, he removes his camera and leaves it unattended for over an hour, presumably while he's inside the home. Because the camera was still capturing an image, this recording wasn't initially flagged by our software. So, we trained a second model to identify "stale scenes" where the recording stays the same for long periods of time. As our models learned and improved, they uncovered lots of suspicious recording gaps. In the end, we documented more than 250 camera obstructions. Moments like these are exactly the situations that body cameras are meant to document, helping ensure that any unlawful behavior is captured and that circumstances surrounding the 122 killings can be properly investigated. Another method we used was an AI system that analyzes audio to detect gunshots. After we trained it specifically for Rio police body cameras and local conditions, the model successfully detected most gunshots in a test set of videos. We were also able to use AI to pull text directly from the videos, like the date, time, location and ID number of the officer wearing the camera. But one of the most striking findings came from what we didn't see. Despite the scale of the operation and the number of deaths, we found no footage showing the killings themselves. NARRATION To understand what was missing, we organized body camera recordings across the operation using extracted timestamps. TEXT ON SCREEN Unusable footage Usable footage NARRATION We found that more than half the officers’ recordings had either ended or had significant gaps by noon. From there, the usable footage continued to decline, just as the operation became most deadly. The missing footage, combined with extensive evidence of camera tampering, suggests that body cameras were deliberately misused to prevent killings from being recorded. Throughout our investigation, AI was one tool out of many. Our team of researchers interviewed witnesses in Rio, visited the neighborhood where the killings took place, analyzed police records and autopsies, verified photographs and videos, and manually reviewed AI findings. What AI provided was speed and scale. It helped us process thousands of hours of footage, connect pieces of evidence, and focus our attention where it mattered most. In other words, AI helped us find needles in a very large haystack. Now, it's up to Brazilian prosecutors to thoroughly investigate both the killings and the decisions that led to such a deadly operation. Those who use disproportionate force or misuse body cameras should be held accountable. To learn more about the events of October 28th and Human Rights Watch’s findings, visit HRW.org and read our investigation, A Strategy of Death. Police officers tampered with body cameras and were responsible for serious investigative failures during an operation ostensibly to arrest gang members in a low-income neighborhood in Rio de Janeiro on October 28, 2025. A year-long Human Rights Watch investigation concluded that police breached Supreme Court orders and their own protocols during Operation Containment, which appeared to be lethal by design. Federal and state prosecutors should initiate criminal and civil proceedings to investigate those responsible for abuses, including senior officials and police commanders. (Rio de Janeiro, October 28, 2026) – Police officers tampered with body cameras and failed to take crucial investigative steps during an operation in a low-income neighborhood in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, on October 28, 2025, Human Rights Watch said in an investigation published today. Evidence indicates police used excessive force and may have intentionally killed scores of men and boys. The investigation, “‘A Strategy of Death’: Investigating Brazil’s Deadliest Police Operation,” documents Operation Containment (Operação Contenção), in which a total of 122 people were killed. This included two children and four police officers killed that day, and a fifth police officer who later succumbed to his wounds. An additional two men were killed in the early morning before the official start of the operation. Eighty-five percent of non-police victims of the October 2025 raid were Black. “A Strategy of Death” Investigating Brazil’s Deadliest Police Operation Read the full investigation here None of the killings were captured in the thousands of hours of body camera footage sent by Rio de Janeiro Military Police to the Public Defender’s Office, which Human Rights Watch reviewed after being granted access. “Human Rights Watch processed thousands of hours of body camera footage and analyzed videos, official investigation files, and autopsy records for every victim, yet crucial questions remain because police failed to properly record killings, preserve crime scenes, or collect crucial data,” said Sophia Jones, open source researcher with the Digital Investigations Lab at Human Rights Watch. “The families of those killed, including police officers, deserve answers and accountability with a thorough, independent investigation.” Human Rights Watch interviewed 41 witnesses, family members, and experts, and analyzed 4,400 hours of body camera footage, 9,000 pages of official investigation files, 122 autopsy reports, court records, and hundreds of videos and photographs. Human Rights Watch analyzed the data using several machine learning models built in-house, followed by manual review and assessment by researchers. Based on Human Rights Watch analysis of data from Rio-based security research lab GENI (Grupo de Estudos dos Novos Ilegalismos or Group for the Study of New Illegalities), nongovernmental think tank Fórum Brasileiro de Segurança Pública (Brazilian Public Security Forum), independent security monitoring organization Fogo Cruzado (Crossfire), and media reports, Operation Containment was the deadliest documented one-day police operation in a country where police forces kill more than 6,000 people per year. Human Rights Watch visited the Complexo da Penha, the site of the operation, six months after the raid and found that the criminal group Red Command (Comando Vermelho)—the target of the operation—continued to impose its rule on residents. Despite the stated goal of carrying out 100 arrest warrants for alleged Red Command members, police records show they arrested only 17 of those for whom they had warrants, although it is not clear whether those are the warrants that justified the operation or other pending warrants. Police did not enter the home of the local Red Command leader, for whom they had a warrant, a Civil Police commander told prosecutors, even though body camera footage shows police moving around it. Despite a state law and a Supreme Court order mandating that police wear body cameras, only about 23 percent of the 2,500 civil and military police officers who participated in the raid did, the Rio de Janeiro government said. Machine-Enabled Forensics How Human Rights Watch used Artificial Intelligence to Analyze Body Camera Footage from Rio’s Deadliest Police Raid Read the methodology here Human Rights Watch analysis of the footage of the 527 military police officers who wore the cameras found widespread tampering and obstruction of their use. Officers left cameras running before the operation, effectively draining batteries; covered lenses; placed cameras where they would not capture officers’ actions; and left cameras in vehicles. Such tampering consistently occurred at key moments, during arrests, shootouts, or while officers entered homes, researchers found. Most tampering was on cameras worn by officers whose units engaged in frontline operations, such as the Battalion of Special Police Operations of the Military Police, the unit deployed to the forested area where the majority of killings took place. Researchers determined that 36 percent of gunshot clusters heard on their cameras occurred when the cameras were obstructed. Body camera footage showed officers assaulting and threatening to kill detainees, including a child, whom they forced to lie down next to a dead body while photographing him. In another recording, an officer tells officers to shoot detainees in the legs if they ran. In a third clip, an officer expressed frustration that body cameras prevented them from killing suspects. Researchers also analyzed or verified hundreds of videos and photographs taken by members of the local community that day. In one series of verified videos, officers pile dead bodies, some with their genitalia exposed, into an armored police vehicle, while joking. “Look how wonderful,” one officer said. “We like this.” While police said they spent months planning the operation, there was no evidence that they made any advance preparations to protect crime scenes and conduct forensic analysis. In addition, Civil Police failed to collect basic information for all but two of the 117 non-police victims, such as the names of police officers and residents who brought some of them to a hospital. Only seven suspects were taken to a hospital and subsequently arrested, compared with 117 people killed by police. That unusually high ratio of people killed to people injured (17 to 1) raises serious questions about whether police prioritized lethal force over arresting suspects. An analysis of victim autopsy reports also points in that direction. Over 40 percent of non-police victims in the reports analyzed were shot in the head, over 60 percent were shot four or more times, and nearly 75 percent were shot at least once on the back. One man was shot and then decapitated. According to forensic experts from the Independent Forensic Expert Group of the International Rehabilitation Council for Torture Victims consulted by Human Rights Watch, the evidence suggests that many were targeted and killed intentionally. In many instances, the trajectory of gunshot wounds was from bottom to top, which can be indicative of execution, such as when an individual is shot while lying down or otherwise incapacitated. Brazilian authorities should ensure a thorough and independent investigation into the planning and decisions by senior officials and police commanders that led to the deadly operation. Rio de Janeiro’s new governor, who will take office on January 6, 2027, should introduce a bill to separate forensic services from the Civil Police. “Our investigation shows police flouted the law and their own protocols during the disastrous raid,” said César Muñoz, Brazil director at Human Rights Watch. “Abusive police practices undermine public security by making communities less willing to collaborate with police, while fueling a cycle of violence that endangers both residents and police officers. Brazil needs new effective public security strategies that uphold human rights.”

Alarming Attacks on Women Politicians. Click to expand Image Ana Elisa Santos Silva of the Workers' Party (PT), the youngest federal deputy elected in Minas Gerais state, poses for a photograph in Divinopolis, Brazil, on October 15, 2026. © 2026 Douglas Magno/AFP via Getty Images Overwhelmed by threats—and fearing for her personal safety Satya Rhodes-Conway the current mayor of Madison, Wisconsin in the US, announced on October 23 that she was dropping her bid for reelection. "The price of being in public office has gotten too high,” she said. Globally, women in public life face alarming levels of political violence, including tech-facilitated sexual and gender-based violence, with little protection or recourse. While research finds chillingly high rates of violence against both women and men in politics, women are at greater risk and face more sexualized and gendered violence. After Australian MP Helen Haines was deliberately hit by a car, doctors had to amputate both of her legs. In South Africa, a bloody campaign season included the killing of party activist Jeanette Magugu and a brutal home invasion against mayoral candidate Nhongo Solo. In Brazil, Ana Elisa Santos Silva and other candidates for public office filed police complaints about death and sexual violence threats on the campaign trail; a city councilor, Iara Pimentel, closed her X account due to threats and was hospitalized after a brick hit her at a rally. Bernadette Greene-Placentia, a US congressional candidate in Arizona, reported that she was attacked while repairing campaign posters and raped. While attackers’ motives are often unclear, the result is the same--women and girls who speak up for their communities increasingly experience gendered violence and threats. After a 15-year-old made a video crudely lambasting India’s Prime Minister, she was inundated with rape and death threats. An Iraqi women’s rights leader who challenged an abusive amendment to Iraq’s personal status law was shot dead outside her home. Technological developments also fuel gendered abuses. Of 720 European Parliament members, 46 women and four men had been depicted in or seen their online presence linked to deep fake sexualized images, according to a 2026 study. In the Asia-Pacific region, 18 percent of participating women parliamentarians faced doxing, according to a study. These crimes are taking place amid a global backlash against women’s rights, with political power for women declining in many countries. After years of progress, the percentage of women national cabinet members globally declined to 22 percent in 2026, from 23 percent in 2024. Experts increasingly warn that political violence deters women from running for office. With growing evidence that women’s leadership brings economic and social benefits, we all lose when women are pushed out of politics.

UAE: UN Secretary-General Candidate Whitewashed Abuses. Click to expand Image Lana Zaki Nusseibeh, representative to the United Nations of the United Arab Emirates, speaks during a UN Security Council meeting at UN headquarters on February 23, 2023. © 2023 John Minchillo/AP Photo (Beirut) – Lana Zaki Nusseibeh, a long-serving UAE diplomat and foreign affairs official, has an extensive record of denying and whitewashing the country’s rights abuses in Sudan and Yemen, Human Rights Watch said today. On October 21, 2026, the UAE formally nominated Nusseibeh to be the new United Nations secretary-general. “For years, Lana Nusseibeh has used her position to vehemently deny and divert attention from the UAE’s war crimes in Yemen and support for the abusive Rapid Support Forces in Sudan,” said Bruno Stagno Ugarte, chief advocacy officer at Human Rights Watch. “Her disinformation about the UAE’s rights record, particularly her dismissal of the UN’s own reports documenting the UAE’s links to the RSF, has seriously undermined justice and accountability for the victims.” Nusseibeh has repeatedly denied that the UAE provides military support to the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) in Sudan, while refusing to address clear evidence to the contrary. The RSF, engaged in a conflict with the Sudan Armed Forces (SAF), is responsible for widespread war crimes and crimes against humanity, including as part of a campaign of ethnic cleansing in the Darfur region. The United Nations Fact-Finding Mission on Sudan concluded that their assault on the North Darfur capital of El Fasher “bore the hallmarks of genocide.” In September 2024, Nusseibeh said in a letter to the editor of The Economist that, “[T]he UAE is not providing weapons or any other support to the Rapid Support Forces or any of the warring parties in Sudan.” The letter followed the publication of the first UN Panel of Experts on Sudan’s report, which included conclusions of “credible allegations” that the UAE was providing military support to the RSF through Chad. A UAE government letter from December 2023 in the report annex claims that flights from the UAE to Chad transported humanitarian assistance to Sudanese civilians. The letter is unsigned but bears the letterhead of the Permanent Mission of the UAE to the UN in New York. Nusseibeh was the head of the UAE’s mission from 2013 until April 2024. In April 2024, in response to accusations from the government of Sudan that the UAE was providing the RSF with military, logistical, and political support, Nusseibeh said in a statement that the “claims were baseless” and affirmed the UAE’s categorical rejection “of the false allegations.” In July 2024, asked by CNN whether the UAE was arming the RSF, Nusseibeh replied: “No, those allegations are categorically untrue. The UAE, as it has done in countless places around the world when there is a humanitarian crisis, has projected humanitarian aid in as quickly as possible and then scaled that way.” In November 2025, as a minister of state, Nusseibeh took part in an Emirati “lobbying blitz” with key European Parliament members that said that the UAE was “playing a constructive role in Sudan” in the lead up to a vote on a resolution condemning atrocities in Sudan, according to Politico. The European Parliament passed the resolution without mention of the UAE’s role in the conflict. Several parliamentary sources told Euronews that Nusseibeh “personally lobbied MEPs [members of the European Parliament] in Strasbourg to influence the content of the resolution.” In a subsequent resolution adopted in July 2026, the European Parliament called out the UAE’s role in support of the RSF and requested sanctions on a UAE company involved in the hiring and transfer of mercenaries to the group. A May 2026 Human Rights Watch report found that Colombian private military contractors, apparently hired by a UAE-based company, transited through UAE military bases before being deployed to Sudan to support and fight alongside the RSF, notably during the forces’ takeover of El Fasher, during which the RSF committed multiple massacres, widespread sexual violence, and a massive abduction-for-ransom racket. The findings provide further evidence that the UAE has been assisting or otherwise substantially contributing to the RSF’s capacity to commit war crimes. In August, the Fact-Finding Mission on Sudan released a report echoing these findings, concluding “that individuals and entities operating from, registered in, or linked to the United Arab Emirates played a significant role in networks involved in the recruitment, financing, transportation and deployment of foreign military contractors and the provision of military-related support benefiting the Rapid Support Forces.” The mission noted “several sources” indicating the presence of Colombian fighters in and around El Fasher before, during, and after its takeover. Human Rights Watch has also documented the RSF using military equipment—Serbian-made shells equipping an attack drone—that had first been sold to benefit the UAE armed forces. On October 27, during an interactive dialogue with UN member states and civil society organizations, Nusseibeh was asked about her denials of findings by the Panel of Experts on Sudan and the Fact-Finding Mission. She did not respond directly to a question about whether she would “continue to reject the findings of the very organization [she] seeks to lead.” Instead, she stated that she had taken a leave of absence from her post as a UAE minister and would refer any questions about the UAE to the UAE government. As permanent representative to the UN, Nusseibeh repeatedly defended the UAE as complying with international law during its intervention in Yemen while dismissing evidence of widely documented abuses. Beginning in March 2015, the UAE played a prominent role in a coalition of countries that conducted military operations in Yemen, including by committing over 30 fighter jets to carry out airstrikes, providing naval ships to enforce the coalition’s maritime blockade, and supporting abusive local forces. In 2016, Human Rights Watch documented 58 unlawful Saudi/UAE-coalition airstrikes, killing nearly 800 civilians and hitting homes, markets, hospitals, schools, businesses, and mosques, and the coalition's use of cluster munitions. In August 2016 and May 2018, Nusseibeh issued statements defending UAE actions in Yemen, claiming that the UAE “takes its own responsibility for upholding international humanitarian law and for protecting civilians very seriously.” The 2018 statement was made a few months before the UAE ordered humanitarian organizations in the coastal city of Hodeida to evacuate despite the immense humanitarian needs, while the Saudi/UAE-led coalition sought to take control of the city from the Houthis. In 2021, the UAE, alongside Saudi Arabia, successfully led a lobbying campaign to end the mandate of the Group of Eminent Experts, an international, impartial, and independent body the Human Rights Council had established to report on rights violations and abuses in Yemen. “Lana Nusseibeh has spent over a decade in roles acting for the UAE government and repeatedly whitewashing their abusive role in Yemen and Sudan, presenting Abu Dhabi as a humanitarian actor while dismissing or obscuring mounting evidence of its role in fueling abuses,” Stagno Ugarte said. “Having dismissed and undermined the findings of the UN’s own reports, UN member states should be asking tough questions about Nusseibeh’s willingness to defend the independence and integrity of the UN and its investigative mechanisms, including those exposing UAE abuses, at a time when these institutions are under attack.”

No Accountability One Year After Tanzania Election Violence. Click to expand Image Protesters use different materials to build barricades and block a road as clashes erupt in Dar es Salaam during Tanzania's presidential elections on October 29, 2025. © 2025 AFP by Getty Images One year after Tanzania’s contested 2025 elections, authorities have yet to make any arrests for human rights violations committed before and during the vote. In the months leading up to the elections, the government intensified its repression of the political opposition, government critics, and the media. Authorities also failed to account for a spate of apparent enforced disappearances, including that of former Tanzanian ambassador to Cuba Humphrey Polepole, who was reported missing just weeks before the elections. Polepole had publicly criticized the ruling party, Chama Cha Mapinduzi, for not being “aligned with safeguarding human rights, peace, and respect for people.” His whereabouts remain unknown. On and after election day, police and people in plainclothes killed hundreds of protesters and bystanders in response to widespread protests and while enforcing a five-day nationwide lockdown. A year on, the fate of many remains unknown as families have reported burying their relatives with no body. Authorities also arrested over 2,000 people they accused of destroying government property and of treason during this period, but later released some. Some, including those interviewed by Human Rights Watch, said police beat them while falsely accusing them of participating in the protests. In November 2025, President Samia Suluhu Hassan established a commission of inquiry to investigate the violence. It concluded that at least 518 people were killed but failed to meaningfully scrutinize the role of security forces. The president has since established another commission that will reportedly investigate the planning of the unrest and excessive and unlawful use of force during the elections. However it remains unclear whether this includes investigating and ensuring the prosecution of people responsible for security force abuses. Meanwhile, the authorities have intensified their crackdown on government critics in recent months. The treason trial of Tundu Lissu, the leader of the main opposition party, Chama Cha Demokrasia Na Maendeleo (CHADEMA), continued this year. On October 21, authorities charged John Pambalu, a CHADEMA official, with treason for allegedly forming an “intention to persuade the public to cause obstruction” of the elections through protests. Treason carries the death penalty in Tanzania. A year since the election violence, families of those killed or missing are still waiting for answers and justice. President Hassan’s government should stop targeting critics and instead ensure credible investigations into disappearances and security force abuses and hold those responsible to account.

Indonesia: Landmark Ruling Allows Civilian Trials of Soldiers. Click to expand Image The Constitutional Court of Indonesia, in Jakarta, October 2023. © 2023 Yasuyoshi Chiba/AFP via Getty Images (London) – The Indonesian Constitutional Court’s ruling requiring reform of the military justice system so that military personnel accused of ordinary crimes can be tried in civilian courts is a major step for justice in Indonesia, Human Rights Watch said today. The government should immediately revise the 1997 Military Justice Law, which has long prevented civilian prosecutions of members of the armed forces for crimes under the Indonesian criminal code, including for serious human rights violations. On October 15, 2026, the Constitutional Court’s nine justices unanimously ruled that the Military Justice Law is conditionally unconstitutional under articles 24(1) and 28D(1) of the 1945 Constitution, which guarantee an independent judiciary and equality before the law. The law will become unconstitutional if it is not amended by October 2028, giving the government a two-year deadline. “The Constitutional Court’s landmark ruling recognizes that Indonesia’s military courts aren’t capable of impartially trying crimes against civilians, as victims and human rights defenders have said for decades, ” said Elaine Pearson, Asia director at Human Rights Watch. “President Prabowo Subianto and the Indonesian parliament should consult with victims and rights groups and promptly amend the military justice law.” Under the 1997 law, civilian police cannot investigate military personnel, with only a few rarely invoked exceptions. Even when soldiers serving in civilian institutions have been accused of crimes under the criminal code, military courts have had jurisdiction over the case. Human Rights Watch found that Indonesia’s military justice system lacks transparency, independence, and impartiality, and has failed to properly investigate and prosecute alleged serious human rights abuses by military personnel. The petitioners challenged articles 9(1), 43(3), and 127 of the law, which allow active duty military personnel to be tried in military courts even for crimes ordinarily prosecuted in civilian courts. The Constitutional Court found that the distinction between military offenses and ordinary criminal offenses must be clearly defined. Justice Enny Nurbaningsih said that when an offense has no military character but accountability for it remains within a command-based system, “there is a structural risk that military’s institutional interests will conflict with the need to ensure independent and impartial legal proceedings.” The Constitutional Court also noted that the military judiciary is not fully integrated into the judicial system overseen by the Supreme Court and urged lawmakers to create a single system. Military judges are active duty soldiers, and investigation, prosecution, and adjudication all take place within the military chain-of-command. Revisions to the Military Justice Law have been pending for decades. As part of structural reforms that followed the end of authoritarian rule under President Soeharto from 1965 to 1998, the 2004 Armed Forces Law made soldiers subject to civilian courts for ordinary crimes. However, that provision would only take effect when a new military justice law was enacted. The Constitutional Court’s ruling imposes a two-year time frame for those revisions, which successive Indonesian governments have deferred. Muhammad Afif Abdul Qoyim, a lawyer from the Indonesian Legal Aid Foundation, told Human Rights Watch: “There is no need to wait two years to revise the Law on Military Justice so that new rules are in line with the Constitutional Court’s ruling.” Serious abuses by Indonesian security forces have gone unpunished for decades because of legal restrictions on civilian investigations and prosecutions under the 1997 law, Human Rights Watch said. On March 12, 2026, military personnel carried out an acid attack against Andrie Yunus, a 27-year-old deputy coordinator at KontraS (Commission for the Disappeared and Victims of Violence), causing burns over 24 percent of his body and possible loss of sight in his right eye. A military court in Jakarta convicted four soldiers in June and sentenced them to 18 months to three years in prison and dismissal from the military. On August 20, a military appeals court reduced the two longest sentences by six months each and overturned their dishonorable discharges. The Judicial Commission has alleged ethical violations by the panel that tried the case at first instance. KontraS said in a statement that the Constitutional Court ruling “closes a legal loophole that has been seen as shielding errant soldiers from accountable law enforcement, and marks a new chapter in upholding the rule of law and completing the mandate of security sector reform in Indonesia.” One of the petitioners in the case is the mother of a 15-year-old boy tortured to death in Medan, North Sumatra, in 2024 by a soldier who was sentenced by a military court to only 10 months in prison, though the maximum penalty is 15 years. In Papua, the military justice system has repeatedly failed victims of violence allegedly committed by military personnel. Under President Prabowo Subianto, a former general dismissed from the military for human rights violations, the military’s role in civilian affairs has expanded. In March 2025, the national legislature passed amendments to the Armed Forces Law to allow active duty officers to hold more government posts. The number of civilian institutions open to serving soldiers—which includes the Supreme Court and the Attorney General’s office—rose from 10 to 14. Lawmakers should prioritize amending the Military Justice Law through an open process with meaningful participation of victims and civil society, Human Rights Watch said. The amended law should clarify investigative and prosecutorial powers and provide a mechanism for transferring cases from military courts to the civilian system. “Justice for civilian victims of military abuses shouldn’t be blocked by an unfair military court system,” Pearson said. “Amending the law on military justice will support efforts begun decades ago to ensure the Indonesian military is a professional, credible institution whose soldiers are held accountable when they commit serious abuses.”

Niger: Prominent Journalist ‘Disappeared’ for 2 Months. Click to expand Image Nigerien journalist Moussa Kaka, former correspondent for Radio France Internationale, February 12, 2007. © 2007 Seyllou/AFP via Getty Images (Nairobi) – Niger’s authorities should urgently disclose the whereabouts of the prominent journalist Moussa Kaka, who was forcibly disappeared two months ago, Human Rights Watch said today. They should ensure his safety and release him unless he has been charged with a valid criminal offense. On August 31, 2026, Kaka, the director-general of Radio Télévision Saraounia and a former correspondent for Radio France Internationale (RFI), left his office in Niamey, the capital, to return home but never arrived, raising immediate concerns. For weeks, his family and colleagues were not able to obtain information about his whereabouts. On September 25, during Niger’s Universal Periodic Review at the United Nations in Geneva, Justice Minister Alio Daouda acknowledged that Kaka was being detained. The minister said Kaka was being held for an alleged “offense” and would “answer before the courts,” but provided no details about the accusation or his place of detention. “Two months after Moussa Kaka vanished in Niger, the authorities have yet to provide his location or explain his detention,” said Ilaria Allegrozzi, senior Sahel researcher at Human Rights Watch. “Kaka’s family will continue to grapple with the uncertainty until the authorities resolve his disappearance.” Kaka is a respected figure in African investigative journalism. For years, he reported for RFI in Niger, until the military junta suspended its broadcasts in 2023. Throughout his career, he has continued his work under successive governments despite the risks and repeated detentions for his journalism. In September 2007, under then-President Mamadou Tandja, the authorities arrested Kaka and accused him of links to ethnic Tuareg rebels, following his extended coverage of the Tuareg rebellion in northern Niger. He spent 379 days in prison before being released in October 2008 following a sustained national and international campaign for his freedom. In October 2025, police in Niamey arrested Kaka along with five other journalists after they announced on social media a press briefing about a government-created solidarity fund intended to support the country’s security forces. The journalists were charged with “complicity in distributing documents likely to disturb public order” under Niger’s broad cybercrime law. All six were subsequently released. Kaka’s recent forced disappearance came amid heightened political tensions following an attempted military coup in Niamey on August 29. After mutinous soldiers attempted to seize power, the junta arrested dozens of suspected soldiers and a former minister. Russian government-controlled Africa Corps forces were called upon to help suppress the mutiny. Kaka’s colleagues and friends have expressed concern that his disappearance may be linked to the junta’s crackdown after the attempted coup. Reporters Without Borders has referred Kaka’s case to the UN Committee on Enforced Disappearances, following an earlier referral to the African Union’s special rapporteur on freedom of expression and access to information. African civil society organizations raised his case at the African Commission on Human and Peoples’ Rights in mid-October in Dakar, Senegal. Journalists and human rights activists across Africa have also called for his release. “Moussa Kaka’s place is not in detention,” said Alioune Tine, a prominent Senegalese human rights defender and former UN rights expert. “His detention is absolutely unjustified and violates Niger’s international human rights obligations, including provisions of the African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights, which Niger has signed and ratified.” Kaka’s case highlights growing concerns about media freedom and political repression in Niger, Human Rights Watch said. Since seizing power in a 2023 coup, Niger’s military junta has solidified its rule, dismantled democratic institutions, and intensified repression of dissidents. They have dissolved political parties, suspended dozens of civil society organizations, detained journalists under a broad cybercrime law, stripped exiled political opponents of their nationality, announced the country’s withdrawal from the International Criminal Court, and extended the political transition without holding elections. The authorities also continue to arbitrarily detain former President Mohamed Bazoum and his wife, and a prominent human rights defender, Moussa Tiangari. Under international human rights law, an enforced disappearance occurs when state agents, or people acting with the state’s authorization, support, or acquiescence, deprive someone of their liberty and then refuse to acknowledge the detention or conceal the person’s fate or whereabouts. Enforced disappearance places victims at heightened risk of torture and extrajudicial execution. It also inflicts profound suffering on families, who are left uncertain whether their loved ones are alive or dead and denied access to justice. “Niger’s authorities should immediately account for Kaka and free him if he hasn’t been fairly charged,” Allegrozzi said. “Governments and international organizations should press the junta to take immediate action in Kaka’s case.”

India: Mass Voter Roll Exclusions Deeply Flawed. Click to expand Image Protesters demand the scrapping of the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls and the resignation of India’s top election official, in Hyderabad, India, on October 24, 2026. © 2026 Jwala Kotesh/NurPhoto via AP Photo The Indian authorities’ removal of over 130 million names from the country’s electoral rolls was arbitrary and deeply flawed.Indian authorities first stripped millions of citizens of their right to vote and are now beating and jailing them for peacefully protesting these rights violations.The authorities should immediately scrap the voter roll revision process that has denied India’s most marginalized people their right to vote and other government services. (London) – The Indian authorities’ removal of over 130 million names from the country’s electoral rolls is arbitrary and deeply flawed, Human Rights Watch said today. In October 2026, tens of thousands of people across India began demonstrating against the Election Commission of India’s Special Intensive Revision (SIR). The process purportedly removed dead, duplicate, or ineligible voters, but has been arbitrary and opaque and has disproportionately excluded women, people living in poverty, religious minorities, especially Muslims, and people from other marginalized communities. In October, the Election Commission submitted an affidavit to the Supreme Court defending its functioning and rejecting all allegations of irregularities. “Indian authorities first stripped millions of citizens of their right to vote and are now beating and jailing them for peacefully protesting these rights violations,” said Elaine Pearson, Asia director at Human Rights Watch. “The authorities should immediately scrap the voter roll revision process that has denied India’s most marginalized people their right to vote and other government services.” The protesters have demanded that the process should be scrapped and that the country’s top election official should resign. The authorities responded with the heavy deployment of security personnel, who committed widespread abuses against protesters and journalists covering the protests. Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP)-led government should immediately end the crackdown on peaceful protests, appropriately prosecute those responsible for abuses, restore every citizen’s right to participate in elections, and establish an independent investigation into allegations of politically motivated interference. Since August, Human Rights Watch has interviewed 70 people in Delhi and the states of West Bengal, Maharashtra, and Karnataka, including 40 people whose families were affected by the SIR process, as well as former election commissioners, lawyers, civil society activists, and a current electoral official. Under India’s Constitution, the Election Commission of India is authorized to revise and update voter rolls, provided that it records its reasons in writing. Ashok Lavasa, a former election commissioner, said that while the commission had routinely updated electoral rolls, it had never before effectively scrapped the voter rolls for the entire country and started the process anew. “The onus of maintaining a clean, updated electoral roll was always on the election commission,” Lavasa said. “It was never on the elector, where he or she had to apply, and if they didn’t apply, their constitutional right would be excluded.” The SIR process began in June 2025 in states with upcoming local elections, requiring voters to show documents proving their eligibility to vote. The process placed a special burden on many in India, especially women and those from socially and economically marginalized communities, who find it difficult to obtain government documents. In addition, the commission adopted arbitrary criteria such as “logical discrepancies” to delete voters who possessed the required documents, modified its rules and forms mid-process without transparency, and used an opaque software system that by its own admission was malfunctioning. The media reported in several states that people had submitted applications seeking to have Muslims deleted from voter lists in bulk. India’s election law allows third parties to object to someone’s inclusion in voter rolls, but it is generally meant for reasons such as death or duplicate entry. Opposition parties and civil society activists allege that the commission has manipulated electoral rolls to benefit the ruling BJP. The Election Commission has not defined the term “logical discrepancies” in any written communication, but Human Rights Watch found that people were arbitrarily excluded for mismatched names, spelling errors, having six or more siblings, or even siblings born less than nine months apart, which would flag most twins. A 26-year-old Muslim tailor with three brothers and four sisters in the South 24 Parganas district in West Bengal said his name was flagged under the “logical discrepancy” list because he had more than five siblings. Five of his siblings were flagged, while three made it into the rolls. “Everyone had documents but despite that our names were deleted,” he said, noting that his family has been on the voter rolls for generations. Even though millions of names had been eliminated from the voter rolls, the Supreme Court in May 2026 ruled that the data did not indicate “systemic disenfranchisement.” And while the court also said that the SIR process did not determine citizenship, BJP state governments in West Bengal and Bihar announced that people whose names were deleted from voter rolls would no longer be eligible for certain government social security programs, including food subsidies. Human Rights Watch found that the authorities have used SIR data to deny government services including passport renewals, social security benefits such as a West Bengal cash assistance program for women, scholarships, and residency certificates needed for college admission. India is a party to the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, which guarantees every citizen the right to take part in the conduct of public affairs, to vote and be elected at genuine periodic elections, and to have access to public services without discrimination or unreasonable restrictions. The United Nations Human Rights Committee, which provides authoritative guidance on the covenant, has stated in its General Comment No. 25 that state authorities are obligated to take effective measures to facilitate and not impose obstacles to voter registration, and they must require that any conditions imposed for exercising the right to vote must be objective, reasonable, and nondiscriminatory. India’s Special Intensive Revision process has been neither reasonable nor proportionate, has imposed unnecessary procedural burdens on millions of people, and could lead to mass disenfranchisement, in violation of India’s international legal obligations, Human Rights Watch said. “The disproportionate removal of Muslims and other groups of voters from the rolls raises serious questions about the fairness of future Indian elections, crucial to holding governments accountable,” Pearson said. “The government should ensure that all those wrongfully removed from voter rolls promptly regain their voting rights and no one loses access to social security and other programs.” An Arbitrary Process India had 960 million registered voters ahead of 2024 general elections. The last intensive revision of voter rolls, between 2002 and 2006, involved enumerators—field workers who collect information about households—conducting door-to-door verification using preliminary lists generated from the then-existing rolls, with strict supervision and monitoring requirements. “It was the inclusive approach and friendly procedure that the Election Commission of India historically followed which enabled the inclusion of more than 98 percent of the eligible adult population in the electoral roll, one of the highest for any functioning electoral democracy,” said Lavasa, the former election commissioner. For the 2025-2026 revision, the Election Commission has instead applied an evolving set of rules across what it describes as three phases of the SIR. In the first phase, in Bihar just months before legislative elections in November 2025, voters had to fill out enumeration forms and provide 1 of 11 documents from an approved list to prove their eligibility. In August 2025, the Supreme Court directed the Election Commission to add a national biometric identity document, the Aadhaar card, to that list. Nearly 4.7 million names were deleted from the state’s voter rolls. In a second phase, in 10 states and 2 union territories, the Election Commission introduced a step called “mapping” in which voters had to trace themselves or a parent to the electoral rolls prepared during the 2002-2006 intensive revision. The poll body also began deleting names from the rolls for what it called “logical discrepancies,” which had no clear definition or legal basis. Voters flagged for a logical discrepancy receive notices and are required to appear for hearings with electoral registration officers mandated to prepare and publish the electoral rolls. “We never knew anything about logical discrepancies during our training,” said a primary school teacher in West Bengal serving as a booth-level officer, who verifies and updates the electoral roll for a specific polling booth. “The process was haphazard and I only received three days of training from election officials before the SIR began,” he said. “And once the exercise began, the rules kept changing.” As the process went on, the rules were often arbitrarily altered. In West Bengal, for instance, the number of voters under suspicion fell from 16.7 million to about 9.5 million within weeks after a public outcry. Muslims, who historically do not vote for the BJP because it promotes Hindu majoritarianism, were disproportionately targeted. In one constituency, Patharpratima in South 24 Parganas, over 92 percent of those deleted were Muslims, though Muslims constitute only 9 percent of the population. Shortly afterward, in the April 2026 election, the BJP won control of the state for the first time, while the Supreme Court effectively said it was acceptable for those excluded not to be able to vote that time so long as they would be added back to the rolls. About 93 percent of the voters in West Bengal whose appeals were decided were eventually restored to the rolls, showing that 9 out of every 10 voters removed from the voter list were wrongfully removed. The Calcutta High Court said, however, that it would take at least 21 years to resolve over 3.4 million appeals to the deletions still pending in the appellate tribunals. In the third and final phase, ongoing in 16 states and 3 union territories, the electoral body modified Form 6 used to enroll new voters, requiring additional information from applicants about whether their parents or grandparents were part of the previous intensive revision. Two election commissioners reportedly objected to these changes, but the electoral body claimed it had Supreme Court permission to add the requirement. The chief justice of India said the court had not approved the change. The Election Commission has also directed states to use Form 6 to reenroll voters who had been deleted from lists, even though these were not new voters but rather those who had voted in previous elections. This required voters to falsely declare that they were applying for the first time, a criminal offense that carries a jail term of up to a year. Misuse of Objection Forms for Bulk Deletions Form 7 allows third parties to object to anyone’s inclusion on the electoral rolls. Media reports show that people in several states filed this form in bulk to systematically object to eligible Muslim voters. When an objection is filed, electoral registration officers may accept an objection if they are satisfied or conduct a hearing by giving notice to the relevant parties. Individual electors were only allowed to file six such forms online, but there was no limit on the number of paper forms they could submit, allowing bulk filing. Opposition leaders and civil society groups accused BJP booth-level agents of misusing the form to file objections in bulk. Until 2023, these agents could file up to 10 forms a day, but they were allowed to file up to 50 forms per day once the SIR was underway in October 2025. In Karnataka, Deputy Chief Minister DK Shivakumar demanded a police inquiry into bulk deletions, and in some districts police cases were filed against BJP workers. In two assembly constituencies in Uttar Pradesh, about 90 percent of the deletion forms were filed against Muslim voters. Five men reportedly linked to the BJP filed 6,500 deletion applications against Muslim voters in Uttarakhand. In May 2026, the Gujarat High Court issued a notice to the state and its election authorities over allegations of targeted deletions. In October, the Election Commission applied stricter limits, allowing each elector to file only 10 forms throughout the claims and objections period. Exclusions Driven by Opaque Software The SIR process uses software to which no one outside the Election Commission has access; the technology has long been opaque and there are reasons to question its reliability. The Election Commission scanned and digitized the paper electoral rolls of 2002 to 2006 and printed the rolls in several Indian language scripts that were transliterated into English by the software, without any publicly established standards to maintain accuracy, the New Delhi-based Internet Freedom Foundation found. This seemingly flawed database provided the baseline for voter eligibility during the first step of the 2025 process, when every voter form was keyed into the system and then traced back to previous rolls. Technologies, including purpose-built or proprietary software designed and deployed for public use, should be subject to public scrutiny, Human Rights Watch said. In December 2025, the office of West Bengal’s chief electoral officer said that the software was malfunctioning because the 2002 data “had not been digitized accurately.” And as Human Rights Watch and others have found, the software has disproportionately flagged names from Adivasi, or indigenous, and Muslim communities for “logical discrepancies,” in part because the spelling of names in such communities is more fluid: for example, Md, Mohammed, Mohd, or Mohammad are variants of the same name; Sk, Shaikh, Sheikh, or Sheik are also equivalents. Md Shamim Akhtar, a former wing commander in the Indian air force, found his name was deleted from electoral rolls in West Bengal in March 2026. He said that he did not receive any notice or hearing even though he had traced his name to the 2002 voter lists. He speculated it was most likely because one of his documents had a period after Md while the other did not, and the software may have flagged that as a discrepancy. His appeal has been pending in the appellate tribunal since April 2026, even though his parents and siblings are included in the final voter rolls. “This is a subversion of democracy,” he said. “If this can happen to me, then what about those who do not have a voice?” Facing Growing Scrutiny In September 2026, the Indian Express published a series of investigations documenting that Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar had made decisions regarding the SIR unilaterally, often over the objections of the other two commissioners. This included decisions to delete names, to add new voters, and to increasingly centralize the electoral roll database. This limited the authority of officers responsible for verifying and finalizing the voter lists, a departure from the decentralized electoral system that the commission has always presented as one of its strongest safeguards. The Election Commission responded by saying differences of views among staff are part of the normal operations of any institution. Petitions challenging the revision process and seeking Kumar’s removal are before the Supreme Court. Former Chief Election Commissioner SY Quraishi said the SIR was “illegal” and called for those responsible in the Election Commission to be “criminally prosecuted.” In October, a current Supreme Court judge called the exercise “intrinsically arbitrary,” while a former Supreme Court judge spoke of Election Commission’s “malfunction.” A judge in the Bombay High Court questioned the purpose of the SIR if citizens were being removed from the voter rolls. Former Indian diplomats and government officials demanded that the exercise be scrapped, saying that it undermined India’s commitment to universal adult suffrage and made a mockery of its democracy. In May, three UN human rights experts warned that the SIR may amount to the instrumentalization of state administrative machinery “for the purpose of political targeting of a religious minority.” Disproportionate Harm to Women, Marginalized Communities The Election Commission’s stated purpose for the SIR was to ensure that “no eligible citizen is left out” and “no ineligible person is included.” Yet existing evidence indicates that large numbers of citizens, disproportionately those from the most marginalized communities, have been wrongly excluded. An analysis of the SIR data by the Hindu found that significantly more women than men have been deleted across the country. Nearly 60 percent of those deleted in Bihar were women. In West Bengal, women constituted over 60 percent of those deleted from the voter rolls and as many as 6 million were unable to vote in the state’s legislative elections. Women made up more than half of the deleted voters in 88 percent of the constituencies in the state and are heavily concentrated especially in areas populated by Muslims, the Scheduled Caste Matua community, and Scheduled Tribes. Issues such as a change in one’s last name, spelling, address, or the ability to map to parents or grandparents have disproportionately affected single women, widows, and those living in poverty. Being marked as “permanently shifted” because of relocation to their husband’s homes after marriage is one of the main reasons women voters have been disproportionately excluded. In the third and final phase of the SIR, the Election Commission stopped disclosing the gender of the voters flagged as suspicious. Several women’s groups wrote to the poll body raising concerns over the large-scale exclusion of women and gender minorities from the exercise. Members of religious minorities, especially Muslims, are particularly likely to be removed from rolls due to third-party objections and being flagged by electoral software for “logical discrepancies.” Documentation by the Kolkata-based Sabar Institute found significant disparities. For instance, Muslims make up 20 percent of the Bhabanipur constituency, while nearly 52 percent of names on the logical discrepancy list are Muslim. A 34-year-old Muslim man in West Bengal said that although his father was on the rolls and he met the mapping requirement, his name was placed “under adjudication” pending verification by judicial officers because he comes from a family with eight siblings, leading the software to flag his registration as containing “logical discrepancies.” However, several of his siblings were included in the lists. During his hearing on February 5, he submitted his Aadhaar card, PAN card issued by the income tax authorities, and voter card, yet his name was deleted three days later. He filed an online appeal on February 12, which remains pending. The process also does not account for people who are estranged from their families. This leaves lesbian, gay, bisexual, and transgender (LGBT) people who are cut off by relatives due to their sexual orientation or gender identity at particular risk of exclusion. Those with severed family relations may not be traced to a relative or have access to documents, such as birth certificates and school records, which families often hold. Several transgender people whose families have abandoned them could not be traced to a relative on the last intensive revision rolls, trans rights activists said. Transgender people who have updated their identity documents face a heightened risk of exclusion. A 2014 Supreme Court ruling recognized transgender people’s right to legal gender recognition, and some transgender people have since updated their records. As a result, older records may carry one name and gender, and newer ones another. The lack of any procedure to reconcile such document mismatches makes it difficult to prove identity, and government-issued transgender identity certificates are not among the documents accepted by election authorities. A 27-year-old Hindu transgender man in West Bengal found his name removed from the rolls after his parents, who were included, refused to give him their voter card details for mapping and deliberately misinformed the booth-level officer of his whereabouts. The officer refused to include his name without his parents’ signature because his other documents reflected his previous name and sex assigned at birth. “I tried contacting my parents after I left home to explain myself to them,” he said. “But they wanted me to leave my partner and marry a man.” Some people whose homes were arbitrarily demolished after authorities claimed the homes were illegal have also been removed from the electoral rolls. In Delhi, about 87 percent of voters were deleted in nine polling stations where homes were demolished, with booth-level officers classifying the displaced voters as “absent/untraceable.” Those displaced were unclear on what address to include on their voter forms. In October, the Delhi Election Commission said it would organize “special camps” for voters whose homes were razed, enabling them to be enrolled. However, these were not uniformly organized across the country. The cost of challenging a deletion, including lost earnings, can make it harder for people with limited incomes, including workers paid by the day living in poverty, to secure reinstatement on the electoral rolls, compounding the barriers they face. In contrast, the authorities have at times bypassed their own official mechanisms to simplify reinstatement of prominent politicians, government officials, and actors. For instance, a notice issued to the Delhi chief minister for a logical discrepancy was resolved within hours without an official hearing. Denial of Access to Government Services, Social Security, and Education In July, the Supreme Court said that SIR data could not be used by the authorities for other purposes. However, information about deleted voters is being used to halt passport renewals and deny access to social security programs, residency certificates for students, and scholarships to children in public schools. In Bihar, the BJP state government removed over 3 percent of names from the public distribution system for subsidized food rations after their names were deleted from the electoral rolls. In May and June, West Bengal authorities published notices saying deleted voters who had not filed appeals in the tribunal would not be eligible for subsidized food grains or direct cash transfers for women under the state’s Annapurna Yojana program, but Human Rights Watch found that even those who had filed appeals were being denied access. A 38-year-old woman in South 24 Parganas district said she had registered for the Annapurna Yojana program in June, had received assistance in July, but then it abruptly stopped. Her name had been deleted from the voter roll in March even though her three siblings were included. She said she appealed the decision, but the state stopped her cash transfers anyway. “I valued that money a lot,” she said. “I used to pay my daughter’s school fees with it.” Another woman, 25, from the same district said she could not register for the cash transfer program after local authorities told her she was ineligible because her appeal was still pending at the tribunal. She had mapped herself to her mother, who was included in the final rolls, but both she and her father were excluded. “Just because our names have been deleted can’t mean that we don’t get any government benefits,” she said. A 45-year-old tailor in West Bengal said his 14-year-old son was denied a government scholarship of 1,200 rupees (about US$13) because both he and his wife had been struck off the rolls. The scholarship is for students from religious minority backgrounds, and school authorities had made parental inclusion on the voter lists an eligibility requirement. “The scholarship was necessary for him,” the man said. The Calcutta High Court in July directed the authorities not to take any “coercive steps” and to continue distributing subsidized food rations and issue government documents to those deleted from the SIR. However, deleted voters have had to continue to go to court to challenge the authorities’ refusal to comply. A 37-year-old man whose appeal is still pending in the tribunal approached the court in April after local authorities refused to issue a residence certificate for him. The man had secured a place in a PhD program at a public university but needed the document to finalize his admission. Using SIR for Unlawful Expulsions In December 2025, Home Minister Amit Shah defended the SIR as a means to “detect, delete, deport” alleged “infiltrators.” However, the Supreme Court clarified in May 2026 that the SIR was not a citizenship test. Indian authorities have also explicitly stated that documents such as passport, voter cards, and Aadhaar are not proof of citizenship. However, a valid voter card is inevitably tied to citizenship because it is presumptively issued only to Indian citizens. Those whose names have been struck off the rolls face heightened suspicion of being undocumented immigrants, a serious consequence given the ongoing unlawful and forcible expulsions of ethnic Bengali Muslims to Bangladesh. Since May 2025, Indian authorities have unlawfully expelled ethnic Bengali Muslims to Bangladesh without due process. After the SIR process was completed, the BJP state government in West Bengal set up detention camps in May 2026 under the “detect, delete, deport” policy and continued arbitrary detentions. In September, police in West Bengal attempted to detain a woman in Bankura district after her name was deleted from voter rolls. “The police said they had been ordered to detain people whose names were excluded from the SIR,” her lawyer said. “They called her an illegal migrant.” Her appeal has been pending in the tribunal since April. A 26-year-old queer Muslim woman in West Bengal’s Hooghly district said that landlords turned down her request to rent apartments and at least three organizations had rejected her job applications because her name was deleted from voter lists. “I feel scared,” she said, “What if they send me to Bangladesh just because my name is not on the voter list?”

Yemen: Houthis Depriving Taizz Civilians of Food, Medicine.
